BreakingNewsTab.title: 'Horrible spike' in flu warning as hospital admissions surge
BreakingNewsTab.text:
A surge in severe cases of flu has prompted health officials in England to urge those most at risk to get vaccinated as soon as possible.

The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) said hospital admission rates had soared by almost 80% over the last week to the highest at this time of year since before the Covid pandemic.

Flu vaccine uptake so far among those aged 65 and over was just under 68% - lower than where it usually was at this time of year, the agency said. The flu can be very serious for those living with some long-term health conditions.

Outgoing chief executive for NHS England, Sir Jim Mackey, talked of how some hospitals had introduced mask-wearing to stem the spread of respiratory illnesses.

Speaking at the NHS Alliance autumn conference, Sir Jim said he was asked to wear a mask for the first time in years during a hospital visit, saying it was "a bit of a shock".

"I think we have more beds occupied with flu than we did this time last year, as we're just about going to that horrible spike in flu," he said.

According to the UKHSA, almost 9.5 million people under the age of 65 in clinical risk groups - including those with lung conditions, kidney or liver disease and diabetes - are eligible for the flu jab.

However, only 34% had received a flu vaccine up to 22 November, leaving almost 7 million without vital protection.

Sir Jim also condemned corridor care in hospitals saying that it had become "embedded" in some parts of the health service.

"It's not something any of us would want for our families, our mothers, our aunties, uncles – whether it's from a safety point of view, or more importantly from a personal dignity point of view," he said, adding there was a need to get a grip and eliminate it."

Suzanna McDonald, who leads the UKHSA's flu programme, said the H1N1 strain was fueling the spread.

She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme the strain "does seem to have picked up a few more changes that we would have expected over the season".

"But the really encouraging news was that last year when we saw a drifted strain, the vaccine still worked very well," she added.

Sir Ciaran Devane, chief executive of the NHS Alliance, representing employers, said: "While the flu season is clearly hitting earlier this year and could add to the strain on NHS services heading into another difficult winter, we are yet to see how or when it will peak.

"The NHS has already had to deal with the challenge of heatwaves this summer, so this could pile yet more pressure on already squeezed services."

Suzanna McDonald urged people to get vaccinated, saying thousands of people die from the flu every year.

Flu levels are expected to increase further as Christmas approaches and people start socialising indoors more.

McDonald also called on those who are ill with respiratory symptoms to practise good hand hygiene by washing hands with warm soapy water, cough and sneeze into elbow or into a tissue, and to stay at home in bed and avoid anyone at much higher risk from catching diseases.

Meanwhile, it emerged that just a little over a third of toddlers in England have had a vaccine so far this autumn on the NHS.

Two and three-year-olds can have the vaccine, given as a nasal spray, for free at GP surgeries and some community pharmacies.

But the UKHSA said just 39% of those eligible had taken up the offer.

School age children usually have the vaccine at school, with a catch-up available in pharmacies from 1 December for those who missed it.

McDonald said: "Please don't dismiss the importance of a flu vaccine for your children.

"It will help keep them out of hospital and even save lives."

This time last year an early increase in flu cases caused real concern across the NHS.

The virus was spreading sooner than expected and the fear was that the numbers would continue climbing right through the always challenging Christmas and New Year period.

As it happened the outbreak peaked early and the bleakest predictions did not become reality.

This time hospital admissions with flu patients are a little higher than 12 months ago after another early surge materialised.

Once again, officials do not know when the peak might be reached.

Adding to the challenges is an increase over the last year in patient numbers with a range of illnesses and conditions, partly explained by the ageing population. That means even more pressure on hospitals and their staff.

A bad flu winter could create significant problems.

BreakingNewsTab.title: GTA 6 crashes into top end of music chart after its record launch
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Grand Theft Auto 6 has been swerving into online feeds and cultural conversations since its record-breaking launch last week.

But one area where the game is really making a dent is the world of music.

Flower In A Hurricane, the single from the game's official soundtrack album by Justice featuring Tame Impala, SZA and King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard, has climbed to number three on the UK's Official Singles Chart.

Go Easy, a new track from Dua Lipa specially recorded for the game, is the highest new entry at 21.

Seven other songs recorded for GTA 6 by artists including Lana Del Rey, Travis Scott and Morgan Wallen also placed in the top 100.

Video game music has topped the UK chart before, when Robbie Williams' It's Only Us, recorded for the FIFA 2000 soundtrack, got to number one.

Run Away With Me, a 2015 song by Carly Rae Jepsen used during a "needle drop" moment in the game's first chapter, has also seen a huge spike in listeners.

It originally peaked at number 58 in the UK 11 years ago, but has re-entered the charts at number 28.

Speaking to BBC music correspondent Mark Savage, Jepsen remembered feeling the track had "something special to it" when she recorded it.

While it's a favourite among some of the singer's most loyal fans, it has never reached the level of recognition as her hits Call Me Maybe and I Really Like You.

"It never got eyes like it's getting right now," she said.

"It's just so lovely to see that happening, it makes me believe in that special feeling that we had."

There are three elements of GTA 6's soundtrack, including an official, double-sided album containing tracks recorded for the game, and an original score composed by electronic duo Justice, due to be fully released in December.

The game also features hundreds of licensed tracks on its in-game radio stations.

Flower In A Hurricane was released as a single in October, giving it time to appear on playlists in the lead-up to the game's debut.

But Mat Ombler, head of partnerships at video game music label Laced Records, says GTA 6's impact on the charts is still impressive.

He says video game soundtracks entering the album charts "isn't unheard of" but "it's incredibly rare to see multiple tracks hitting the singles charts".

Ombler likens the spike in streams of Jepsen's track to the boost Kate Bush's Running Up That Hill got from its inclusion in Netflix hit Stranger Things.

"Both tracks are part of a huge cultural moment, but I'd argue that GTA's usage of Run Away With Me is more impactful... where the music responds according to what you're doing during a key story mission," he says.

Ombler thinks the chart impact of GTA 6 highlights "the growing importance and cultural impact of video game soundtracks as a whole".

"Over 40 million people will spend the coming weeks and months listening to more than 800 tracks featured in the in-game radio stations, possibly hundreds of times," he says.

"They'll discover new music in genres they might never have engaged with otherwise, and this music will stick with them for the rest of their lives."

Only One by New York band Fcukers appears on the official GTA 6 soundtrack and has already had more than one million streams on Spotify.

The group's singer Shanny Wise tells Newsbeat: "It was actually one of the songs we recorded when we were making our album, but it didn't end up making the album."

"We felt like the vibe of it maybe was too much of an outlier," adds bassist Jackson Walker Lewis.

"But when the GTA thing came around... I felt like it perfectly fit."

Lewis says the band didn't know they'd made the official soundtrack album until the tracklist leaked in the days leading up to the game's release.

"The one thing I'll say is, Rockstar operates very fluidly behind the scenes," says Lewis.

"They can change their mind last-minute. I think that's what makes them so good at what they do is because they have flexibility."

Steven Ellison, better known as Flying Lotus, points out the GTA series was already an established cultural phenomenon.

Millions of players heard the US producer, DJ, film-maker and rapper hosting FlyLo, one of GTA 5's in-game radio stations.

He also curated its tracklist - a job he confesses was made easier by the series' profile.

"People just wanted to have any involvement at all," he says.

"It was like: 'Who do we want? Who don't we want?' It was incredible."

He says the role gave him an opportunity to "shine a light on musicians from LA", his hometown, and the inspiration for the game's fictional location Los Santos.

It also influenced his own musical taste, he says.

"I remember when I played GTA: Vice City and it was the first time I actually listened to Africa by Toto.

"I was like: 'Man this song is awesome'. I didn't really know it before."

That curated experience, according to Ellison, is a big part of the appeal, and why the game can generate surprise hits out of neglected songs.

"It's so hard to get an experience like that nowadays with the way we listen to music and find music," he says.

"So this is kind of like that experience from back in the day where you're actually being put on to something by hanging out with people and then someone plays a track.

"It's that genuine connection that I think is possible with this."

Additional reporting by BBC Newsbeat reporters Jordan Kenny and Naomi Clarke.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Capsized tanker carrying 7,000 tonnes of diesel to be towed away from Ibiza
BreakingNewsTab.text:
A tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel which capsized off the holiday island of Ibiza on Thursday will be towed to the port of Cartagena, officials in Spain say.

All 17 of the Malta-registered Med Emre's crew members were rescued but the chief engineer later died in hospital. Six people were treated for minor injuries.

There had been concerns of a major oil spillage in the western Mediterranean but an inspection showed that the ship's fuel tanks are intact. An investigation is under way into what happened.

The vessel had been travelling from Algeciras near Gibraltar to Barcelona and is expected to arrive in Cartagena on Monday in what is being seen as a challenging rescue operation.

In a statement on Friday, the Spanish transport ministry said the tanker would be towed to Cartagena "as it is the only one [port] that meets the technical requirements to carry out cargo extraction and repair work".

Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez told Cadena SER radio network he hoped the tanker could be taken to port "in the coming hours, in the coming days".

"The information suggests that, indeed... this leak is not happening", he added.

The Spanish authorities provided no details about how the diesel would be extracted.

Meanwhile, pictures have emerged showing emergency workers inspecting the tanker's hull off the Balearic Islands.

Any possible environmental damage is being assessed by air and pollution control vessel Clara Campoamor, which is owned by Spain's national maritime rescue service.

Elena Delgado, maritime captain of the port of Valencia, earlier told news agency AFP that a small slick which had formed around the vessel had "disappeared".

"The situation is stabilised," she said, adding that further inspections would be carried out.

Regional emergencies director Pablo Gárriz said the tanker had not completely sunk as originally reported. The vessel remains partially submerged.

The Med Emre capsized 25 nautical miles (46 km; 28 miles) from Ibiza's coastline and 57 nautical miles from Valencia.

Rescuers in Valencia received a distress call late on Wednesday, according to Spanish media.

Minutes later, the vessel reported a leak and the crew said it was leaning at a 90-degree angle. It capsized in the early hours on Thursday.

Ibiza's marine environment was added to the Unesco World Heritage List in 1999. In particular, it is home to dense prairies of Posidonia oceanic seagrass, which is found only in the Mediterranean basin and plays a vital role in supporting local marine biodiversity.

In 2002, Spain experienced one of its worst environmental disasters when the Prestige oil tanker ran into trouble off Galicia's coastline, in the country's north-west.

More than 60,000 tonnes of heavy fuel oil spilled into the sea.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Paul Mackenzie: Kenyan doomsday cult leader convicted over further 123 deaths
BreakingNewsTab.text:
A court in Kenya has convicted the leader of a doomsday Christian cult of the manslaughter of 123 of his followers.

Paul Mackenzie was found guilty in Mombasa of ordering his followers, all adults, to fast to death in Shakahola forest near the coast between January 2021 and September 2023.

Earlier this month Mackenzie was jailed for 200 years for murdering 191 people, all but one of them children, in the same mass killing.

Mackenzie had pleaded not guilty to manslaughter and one of his lawyers said he would appeal against the conviction after sentencing, Reuters news agency reports.

Warning: This article contains details which some people might find distressing.

The court also convicted 29 others including Mackenzie's wife, Rhoda Mumbua Maweu, of their part in the manslaughter.

Sixty defendants were acquitted. The Director of Public Prosecutions indicated that an appeal would be launched against their acquittal.

The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest, near the Indian Ocean coast.

The court found Mackenzie had "systematically persuaded his followers to fast until they died", Kenya's Office of The Director of Public Prosecutions said in a statement on Friday's verdict, which it described as "the final conviction" in the cases against him.

"Children were to go first, then women and then men, with Mackenzie himself meant to die last," the office said.

The prosecution argued that Mackenzie and his accomplices had acted together as part of a suicide pact to fast to death in order to "meet Jesus".

Witnesses testified that he had preached that education, medicine and ornaments were sinful.

Those who opposed his teachings were beaten to death, according to the verdict in his trial for the murder of 191 people.

The defendants had claimed that the victims had fasted out of their own free will.

FinanceTab.title: Why Trump's new tariffs are less of a threat
FinanceTab.text:
There was none of last April's fanfare, the Rose Garden reveal, the gameshow blue board or "Liberation Day" rhetoric surrounding Trump's tariff announcement this week.

Instead there is something rather tentative about this latest exercise with talk of further negotiations.

"We expect to have a broad, even a plurilateral negotiation to talk about excess capacity and how to resolve it," US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC.

Around the world the view is that this week's announcement is an attempt to shore up the domestic legal underpinning of these tariffs, more than a fundamental change in the Trump trade agenda.

The tariffs are also not due to come in until January or possibly February, after a period of consultation. There has already been eight months of process and hearings, and the rates announced are upper ceilings, often up for negotiation. It's quite the contrast to the overnight shock meted out to the world last April.

Still, the US is making the argument that large swathes of the rest of the world, including allies, are harming the US goods trade position by supporting their own industries. This is the basis for the tariffs, in large part replacing the previous tariffs justified on "forced labour" provisions.

The UK, which was unaffected by the new tariff announcements, remains caught by the forced labour provisions, albeit at a rate of 10% extra on global tariffs. There was no move in response to the UK's digital services tax.

It means for many important countries there are now two legal bases upon which the Trump tariffs rest, after the Supreme Court struck down the original emergency basis earlier this year. A group of 25 states has taken the Trump administration to court to strike down the forced labour tariffs.

The tariffs will have to be finalised under a Democrat Congress, which has influence, but not power. The Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries said this week that the new House would in its first 100 days "move aggressively to… repeal the Trump tariffs".

The Chinese rate of 20% is the truce rate from last year's Trump-Xi deal. The truce is due to expire in mid-January. Beijing's response was muted, no retaliation, criticism of industrial overcapacity as a "false issue", and a call to implement the Xi-Trump deal. The leverage over China has weakened, with the US share of its exports dropping to around 10% this year, down from 15%, just two years ago, and 19% in 2018.

FinanceTab.title: UK to pay 'participation' fee to deliver EU deals
FinanceTab.text:
The UK will pay a "participation fee" to the EU as part of the deals agreed by Andy Burnham, according to legal documents.

The surcharge will go towards the running costs of EU agencies and systems required to deliver two of the agreements unveiled by the prime minister last week.

It will be paid in addition to a contribution towards costs that broadly mirrors how EU members contribute to the bloc's shared budget, the documents show.

The government has sought to contrast the financial costs of the deals against their overall effect on the economy, which it estimates will receive an eventual boost by billions a year due to increased trade.

The government is yet to publish an estimate of overall additional costs, but officials said they expected them to be in the low tens of millions per year and "massively outweighed" by predicted economic gains.

British ministers had already said they were prepared to pay towards administrative costs required to implement deals to re-link the UK to the EU's carbon trading regime, and align Britain with the EU's food standards.

Now, details of how the payments will be calculated have been revealed in treaties to deliver the two agreements, which are meant to take effect during 2028.

Legal text for a third agreement agreed last week, on youth visas for 18 to 31 year olds, is expected to be published in the coming days.

According to the treaties, the payments will be made as a share of the running costs of three EU agencies, as well as various systems that will be used to implement the food standards and emissions deals.

The bulk of the payments, to be made in euros, will come in the form of an "operational contribution" in proportion to the size of the British economy compared to that of the EU.

This broadly mirrors the way in which EU member states split the cost of their main contributions towards the bloc's overall budget.

But in addition, the UK will also pay a "participation fee" set at 4% of its main contribution figure.

The government has pointed to the 2021 Brexit trade agreement negotiated by the Conservatives, which also applied an additional surcharge to UK contributions towards the cost of relevant EU programmes.

However, any additional contributions are likely to be seized upon by opponents of the latest deals.

Ministers had declined to enter into specifics of the fees during negotiations on the treaties. On Sunday, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the latest deals agreed by Burnham were "not about cost to the taxpayer".

It comes as the government published separate legislation granting it broad powers to incorporate new EU laws required to implement the agreements, without having to hold a full vote each time.

The food standards deal in particular will mean Britain will have to align with scores of current EU food-related laws that have been updated since Brexit, along with future rules in these areas.

The government argues the new powers are required because it would be impractical to run a full parliamentary process each time UK legislation needs to be updated to make the agreement work.

But it has prompted criticism from opposition parties, because the UK no longer has voting rights at the EU to shape European legislation.

The government argues the UK will get a say on new rules, with the treaty texts confirming British experts can be consulted when new EU laws are being drawn up, with the UK granted "observer" status in certain meetings.

But Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Burnham was showing "disdain for the democratic process" by asking for a "blank cheque to install and enact EU law".

"The prime minister is telling MPs to hand him extraordinary powers whilst having no idea what the EU will actually agree to," she added.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has argued the Burnham's deals would take Britain back into "much of the European Union's single market".

He added: "European economies are not growing as fast as ours. The idea that getting closer to the EU will mean growth for us is a myth."

FinanceTab.title: My self-care ritual is a meal at a fancy restaurant - on my own
FinanceTab.text:
Catherine Smith is perusing the menu at a high-end Mediterranean restaurantshe has been excited to try. She has a new outfit on, and as she sips her rosé, shelooks across at the empty seat opposite - bliss.

"I think what is so special about solo dining is that you don't have to wait for people to make those plans. You can go out and do them yourself," says the 23-year-old.

The self-confessed foodie is part of a growing trend of people booking tables for one - not because they're away with work but as a treat.

As food trends analyst Charles Banks puts it: "[Eating alone] is becoming an intentional act, a little pocket of independence, indulgence and self-care."

We spoke to solo dining fans and hospitality industry experts about how the trend is shaping the restaurant experience and asked if you would book a table for one.

Catherine, from Yorkshire, began dining solo at university and now does it at least once a month, choosing high-end restaurants she would not usually go to with friends and family.

She has been to a range of places both in the UK and abroad, doing "lots of research" to find new spots, typically spending £100 to £200 per meal.

"I think because a lot of my friends are vegan or vegetarian, I find that difficult sometimes because I'm quite a big meat eater," she says.

"I find it nice to be able to go out and pick a restaurant where I haven't had to scour through the menu to make sure that it's suitable for them."

Catherine says the sense of freedom she gets from picking where and when she eats "feels empowering".

"It definitely feels like not only a form of self-care but also a form of female liberation."

Online booking platform OpenTable says it covers more than 5,000 restaurants in the UK. It says solo dining makes up the smallest proportion of its bookings in the UK but it is the fastest-growing category.

Figures from 1 January to 31 August this year saw a rise of 23% in solo bookings compared to the same time period a year ago. It did not provide the data to the BBC to verify.

Nishi Singh was an avid solo diner when she lived in London, but found it wasn't widely accepted after moving to Delhi.

"Someone approached me and said that they assumed I'd been stood up," she tells BBC World Service's The Food Chain podcast.

"It sparked a conversation about the culture around solo dining in Delhi and I was really shocked to hear that it's not really something people do."

A couple of days later, she started documenting her solo dining experience on social media.

"Quite a lot of people have reached out and said that this is something they'd like to do and they're too scared to do it themselves," she says.

Banks, joint managing director of The Food People, a food trends and ideas agency, says that while solo dining isn't a "new consumer behaviour", changes in society mean it has become "almost aspirational".

But he notes that not every restaurant has welcomed the trend.

"A single diner could therefore feel like an inefficient use of a table rather than a customer the restaurant actively wanted."

"We want people to feel comfortable in these sorts of environments, being able to walk in on their own," he says.

He has hired staff with "bigger personalities" to engage customers in conversation but they also know when to leave diners alone if they want a more solitary experience.

Catherine urges anyone who fancies solo dining to give it a go.

"Food is a great way to bring people together, but it's also a great way to have good experiences on your own.

"I think with time, people will see and will start to accept it as something that's more normal."

Additional reporting by Jemma Crew and Emma Jackson.

FinanceTab.title: Is Poundland's US owner to blame for its collapse?
FinanceTab.text:
The blame game for the demise of Poundland is in full swing.

The number one target is US-based Gordon Brothers who bought the discount chain for £1 and have taken nearly £20m out of the business already.

Gordon Brothers stand to get paid back a further £22.5m, as their share of an existing £30m loan is set to be one of the first debts that the administrators will have to pay out of the proceeds of any sale of the business in whole or in part.

The team running Poundland blame the owners for strangling their ability to turn the business around, saying that their access to Poundland's own cash was restricted, leaving them unable to fully restock ahead of the crucial Christmas period.

They point to improving sales over recent months as proof the business had a future.

MPs also laid into the US firm with members of the Business Committee accusing it of "predatory capitalism" and "asset stripping".

Unsurprisingly perhaps, Gordon Brothers dispute a lot of how they have been characterised.

First, they insist that they lent the business £85m to try to keep it alive for the 17 months since they bought it. Without them, this collapse would have happened in June last year.

The £20m taken out of the business since then has mostly been interest on that loan.

Despite brief periods of sales growth compared with a year earlier, Poundland was not generating enough cash to sustain itself. Sales were forecast to be £115m lower than predicted when Gordon Brothers bought the business - more than offsetting a £100m cost-cutting programme.

Like other retailers Poundland was hit by rising labour costs, employment taxes and business rates.

In the end, argue Gordon Brothers, none of the potential buyers could meet their terms and prove they had the money and expertise to make a go of it.

Such is the discrepancy between the two versions that the chair of the Business Committee wants Gordon Brothers and the management back in front of them to get to the truth.

It is still possible that a bidder may emerge in the coming hours and days to save the business as a whole but most industry observers think that looks unlikely.

Julie Palmer of insolvency specialists Begbies Traynor told the BBC: "This sort of direction of travel seemed somehow inevitable. Obviously, if one of those interested parties steps up and buys the whole business and assets, that's the best, quickest and cleanest outcome. I think realistically, though, there is a chance now that there will be a breakup."

Like previous busts such as Woolworths, BHS and Wilko, many of these stores will find new owners and they will need local, experienced staff.

But none of that will be much comfort to those workers facing grave uncertainty a month before Christmas, when they should be at their busiest and most needed.

Gordon Brothers specialise in situations of commercial distress. When they take on a distressed company, they try to make sure that the worst possible outcome is still one that makes money for them.

In this situation, the worst outcome would mean they get paid back £22.5m, earn interest on the loan they provided the company (secured against the company assets) and a few other miscellaneous fees.

Little wonder then that many people say they had little incentive to strain every sinew to secure a buyer. They argue they kept a business that would have collapsed last June going for another 17 months, which extended employment for thousands of workers.

But if, as some retail veterans have told the BBC, Gordon Brothers never really intended to turn this business around, why would the previous owners PepCo give them a no-lose gamble? Why didn't they do what Gordon Brothers are doing - profiting with no risk?

The answer is simple: Pepco have other businesses, which could have got tangled up in the administration of Poundland.

FinanceTab.title: Millions of people to see average monthly mortgage payments rise by £100
FinanceTab.text:
More people face higher mortgage repayments when they roll off a fixed deal than previously estimated, new figures from the the Bank of England show.

About 6.5 million owners are forecast to see their monthly repayment jump by £100 on average when they move onto their next deal by the end of 2029, new data in its Financial Stability Report reveals.

That is more the double the £45-a-month hike that the Bank estimated in its last report in July.

In the shorter term, about one million of those homeowners, who are on mortgage rates below 3% and due to refinance by the end of next year, will see an average £200 increase in their monthly repayments.

For borrowers, the interest rate on a fixed mortgage does not change until it expires, usually after two or five years, and a new one is chosen to replace it. The vast majority of homeowners and buyers have this kind of mortgage.

Since the Iran war began, global economic uncertainty has been pushing up the cost of deals, with the average rates on two and five year fixed mortgages at their highest for about three years.

On Thursday, the average rate on a two-year deal was 5.99%, and at 6% for a five-year deal, according to the financial information service Moneyfacts.

Analysts have described the situation as "brutal" for homeowners coming to the end of their fixed deals.

However, the Bank's report points out that the average £100 increase in monthly repayments was half the rise experienced by those refinancing during 2023 and 2024.

Dawn Fazackerley-King is a Pilates instructor who lives near Ipswich and has previously spoken to the BBC about her struggles with the cost of living.

She was on a five-year fixed deal at 1.4%, which she took out in January 2022. But the mother-of-two is about to refix for two years and the best deal she can find is a 5.69% loan. That will push her costs up by about £200 a month.

FinanceTab.title: When will Poundland shops close? Five key questions answered
FinanceTab.text:
Poundland has collapsed into administration, leaving the jobs of its 11,000 staff in doubt in the run-up to Christmas.

The company has appointed consultancy Alix Partners to oversee a sale of part or all of the discount retailer, with questions remaining about the future of the company.

This is the question that is most difficult to answer.

Poundland shops will remain open as usual for now. The firm collapsing has acted as a reset in the process of selling it.

Administrators are looking to either sell the business as a whole, or to break it up, which is the more likely outcome.

When Poundland was still a going concern, Irish property firm Martin Property Group made an offer for it. But a source said the group was now "unlikely" to make a fresh bid due to "irreparable harm" to the brand from the administration process.

Before the collapse, Fortress, which owns rival budget chain Poundstretcher, was interested in buying about 200 of the stores, and wanted to keep those trading under the Poundland brand.

But Fortress's position at the moment is unclear. The BBC understands it is considering selling Poundstretcher, a move first reported by Bloomberg.

A decision on Poundstretcher could come before the end of this week. However, Fortress has declined to comment.

That depends on who you ask.

When the chain was sold by Pepco last year for £1 it was struggling. It suffered a £68m loss that year.

Poundland's managing director Barry Williams said Poundland had been seeing a "strong recovery" and recorded a profit by one measure in the first nine months of this year.

Poundland's management paint a picture of a retailer that was turning a corner until the owner, US investment firm Gordon Brothers, pulled the plug on funding for day-to-day expenses such as buying stock.

The Usdaw union, which represents shopworkers, claim the owners forced Poundland into administration.

Labour MP Antonia Bance said she was "pretty appalled" by the conduct of Gordon Brothers over the past few weeks, and that it was going to make much bigger profits by breaking up the business rather than by keeping it going.

However, Gordon Brothers insisted the business was only turning a profit on paper, and had missed budget forecasts.

A spokeswoman said while the management team had made £100m in cost reductions, the business had moved from a £70m loss to "around break-even".

"Break-even is different from generating the cash needed to buy stock, invest, and withstand increasing economic pressures," the spokeswoman said. "A few good weeks do not make a turnaround."

Poundland repeatedly missed budget targets over the year, the spokeswoman added.

Gordon Brothers was concerned that as inflation goes up next year, those pressures would have helped to make the business unviable, it said.

And Julie Palmer, managing partner at insolvency agency Begbies Traynor, said Poundland's collapse "seemed somehow inevitable" due to challenges facing retailers - including higher costs to employ staff.

Stores are still trading while the administrators work out if the business is viable.

The funds locked up by Gordon Brothers - at the last count about £70m - have now been released by the administrators.

This has turned the taps back on, so staff will continue to be paid in the run-up to Christmas, and so will suppliers.

But here's the catch: the administrators have a legal obligation to maximise value for "secured" creditors. It means the owners, Gordon Brothers, are at the head of the queue for being paid back the loans that were stumbling blocks in the negotiations.

But more importantly for staff, if the administrators can get more value by breaking up the business than by selling it as a whole, then that is what they have to do, even if the business would be viable.

If the business is broken up and its stores are sold off, the new owners would not be obliged to keep staff on.

That depends on what happens next.

Administrators will have to get the best value for creditors, which could mean selling the business as it stands.

But if Poundland is broken up, administrators could sell the brand without the stores, or the brand along with some of the stores, or the stores without the Poundland brand, to other retailers.

As a result there could be fewer discount stores on the High Street, providing less incentive for other retailers to keep prices down.

"Poundland is a place they go on the High Street to get bargains and... given the cost of living challenges we face, that is of concern to us in government," Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, told the BBC on Thursday.

Poundland's customers may well turn to rival budget retailers in the hunt for bargains.

FinanceTab.title: Norse Atlantic suspends all flights as it faces potential collapse
FinanceTab.text:
The Norwegian low cost carrier Norse Atlantic Airways has suspended all flights as it rushes to resolve what it warned is a critical financial situation.

The airline said if no solution can be found, it intends to file for bankruptcy.

It uses a fleet of 12 Boeing 787 aircraft on long-haul routes from a number of European airports, including London Gatwick, Rome and Oslo.

Prior to the suspension of flights, it was advertising services from London to Orlando, Cape Town, Bangkok and Phuket.

One aircraft was meant to depart London for Orlando this morning, while another was meant to arrive from Cape Town this evening.

The suspension has also affected Pakistan International Airlines, which had been leasing aircraft and crews from Norse Atlantic.

PIA was forced to cancel services from London to Islamabad and from Manchester to Lahore last night.

In a statement on social media, PIA said all UK flights from today would be operated by aircraft from its own fleet.

Londoner Fred was due to fly to Cape Town with Norse Atlantic next week for a friend's wedding, but has decided to change his plans.

"Yesterday the exact same flight I was going to get was cancelled, so I was worried" he told the BBC's Your Voice. "I sent an email to Norse and have had nothing back".

He decided to rebook with a different airline, which cost him an extra £1,000.

Another traveller, Claire from Herefordshire, is currently on holiday in South Africa with her daughter.

"We are due to fly home on Sunday and are now looking at a really expensive flight back," she said.

"We have tried contacting Norse but have been given an automated response saying someone will get back to us within three business days."

Consumer group Which? advised Norse Atlantic customers to not cancel their flights as the airline has not collapsed. Doing so removes passengers' right to a refund.

Rory Boland, Which? travel editor, said: "If Norse does go bust, whether you get a refund depends on how you booked and paid. If you booked directly with Norse, you may be able to claim a refund via your credit card provider, or possibly your debit card."

Those stuck abroad should contact insurers, while those with package holidays reliant on Norse Atlantic flights should contact their tour operator, he added.

Norse Atlantic Airways was set up in 2021 as a low-cost long-haul carrier.

It entered the market as a successor to Norwegian, which withdrew from long haul routes as a result of the Covid pandemic.

But it has struggled to make money, and its problems worsened this year, as fuel prices rocketed due to the war in Iran.

Unlike many other European carriers, Norse Atlantic does not hedge its fuel bills by buying supplies in advance at fixed prices.

This left it fully exposed when prices soared, with the cost of fuel roughly doubling at one point. Prices remain significantly higher than they were before the conflict began.

In the first half of the year Norse Atlantic made a loss of $94.6m.

In a statement to the Oslo Stock Exchange on Wednesday, the airline said its financial situation was critical, and it needed to find short term funding to continue its operations.

After suspending flights, the company said it was in discussions with investors regarding a possible takeover that "would include a financing solution".

However, it said if short term funding could not be found quickly, "it is the Board's intention to file for bankruptcy".

Norse Atlantic had been looking for a buyer since July.

Its potential collapse follows the failure of Spirit Airlines in May. The US-based low cost carrier was another airline left exposed when jet fuel prices soared, as US airlines typically do not hedge their purchases.

If Norse Atlantic were to fold, it would be another major setback for the low-cost long-haul model, which has typically proved popular with passengers but difficult to sustain financially, especially on transatlantic routes.

Additional reporting by Rozina Sini

FinanceTab.title: Drivers over 70 face eye tests every three years under new plans
FinanceTab.text:
Over-70s will have to take eye tests every three years or face losing their driving licence under new road safety plans.

Mandatory eyesight tests are part of the Department for Transport's (DfT) road safety strategy, expected within weeks.

Around 6.5 million over-70s hold drivers' licences, with 1.6 million of those aged 80 or over.

To drive legally in the UK, you must be able to read a standard number plate from 20 metres away, wearing glasses or contact lenses if required.

Government sources told the BBC ministers will recommend over-70s be made to regularly prove their eyesight meets the minimum standards. Those who do not, or who fail to meet the minimum standard face losing their licence.

The change follows a consultation which launched early last year, set to recommend a shake-up of the rules for older drivers.

Under the current rules, over 70s have to renew their licence every three years, but only have to self-certify that their sight.

Dennis Reed, of campaign group Silver Voices, which represents older people, said it was "discriminatory to just pick an age out of the hat and say 'everybody over 70 has to go through this, but nobody else does'".

But he said the group is not opposed in principle to regular eye tests for older drivers.

FinanceTab.title: Brazil pushes back on Emmanuel Macron calling its meat 'doped'
FinanceTab.text:
Brazil says it "regrets" a statement by French President Emmanuel Macron who called Brazilian meat "doped".

France's leader made the comment while meeting representatives of farming unions on Wednesday, during which he celebrated EU restrictions on imports of Brazilian meat and poultry which took effect in September.

In its statement, the Brazilian government said Macron's statements "spread misinformation and contradict the widely available technical and scientific evidence on animal protein production in Brazil".

Macron's comments come as part of a trade row between the EU and Mercosur - the South American trade bloc. The EU banned Brazilian meat, poultry and other animal products owing to the use of antimicrobials in farming.

In its defence, Brazil said it had supplied animal protein to the EU for decades and that it exported meat to 177 markets. It added the country had a rigorous sanitary control system, corroborated by a recent European audit, and observed stringent environmental requirements.

Macron, in his opening remarks in the meeting with the agricultural sector representatives at Élysée Palace, said he was "proud of the fight we led" against Mercosur.

"And the 'doped' meat, if I may put it that way, or rather meat from Mercosur countries, especially Brazil, that was arriving in our ports and therefore entering our markets without complying with our rules, was ultimately banned," he said.

Brazil said it was concerned about the "clearly political nature" of recent EU restrictions, and urged France to reconsider its position "in light of scientific evidence".

Affirming its partnership with France was important, the country emphasised that "in the face of protectionist pressures, the best interests of the bilateral relationship must prevail, always guided by mutual respect and reciprocity".

Brazil is a massive exporter of meat, especially beef - some $1.84bn (£1.4bn) of which went to EU markets alone in 2025, according to Brazil's agricultural ministry.

FinanceTab.title: ‘It’s not helping’: calls for guardrails and regulations as AI use rises at US retailers
FinanceTab.text:
As millions of Americans begin holiday shopping this Black Friday, consumers and workers alike are already seeing how artificial intelligence is reshaping the retail landscape.

Anna, a cashier in a southern Oregon Walmart and leader with United for Respect, who requested to remain anonymous for fear of retaliation, criticized the implementation of AI at Walmart and its effects on workers.

According to Anna, AI is used for human resources tasks such as scheduling, assigning attendance disciplinary points, and through a safety alert system that she says is often inaccurate and often pulls her away from customer service interactions.

“During the course of a day on a given shift, I will get at least 10 or 15 safety alerts on my phone. I can’t move on through the app until the safety alert’s clear.” she said. “It’s very annoying when you get them. I need to go over here to help this young lady who’s crying her eyeballs out because she needs a pregnancy test, and I can’t get in to get her pregnancy test because I have to clear a stupid alert.”

She explained she has to take a photo and upload it after completing a safety alert, noting alerts can often mistake a shadow, a sticker, or something else as an actionable item, or will be flagged to an associate when it is a maintenance issue.

“If there is something that I clearly see that is on the floor, I’m going to pick it up. I’m not that ignorant to not to pick it up, but I don’t need an AI telling me to do it,” she added. “It’s not helping. This thing is supposed to be working with us and to help us and things like that. I don’t see how this is, because it’s not.”

In September 2026, several hundred Walmart workers had signed on to an open letter calling for the company to put workers first as it rolls out the use of AI in stores.

Walmart investors overwhelmingly voted down a proposal for a report on how the Walmart workplace is being affected by AI and automation in June 2026. A Walmart spokesperson cited an internal June 2026 survey where 84% of Walmart workers claimed they were confident using digital tools.

“Walmart’s approach to AI is, and always has been, people-led and tech-powered,” a Walmart spokesperson said in an email. “We use AI to serve our customers and members and better support associates – not to replace their judgment, experience, or expertise. Like any technology, these tools evolve over time, and feedback from the associates who use them helps us continually improve the experience and build practical tools that are useful on the floor.”

The use and implementation of AI in the retail industry is expected to continue to grow, according to industry leaders.

According to a survey of 56 AI leaders at US-based retailers published in December 2025 by the National Retail Federation, most retailers have or are implementing AI in a variety of uses, with plans to increase investments and implementation over the next few years.

About 75% of retailers surveyed reported implementing AI tools for coding and app development, 73% for office productivity tools, 66% for cybersecurity and fraud development, 59% reported preparing or implementing AI for supply chain and warehouse operations, and 45% reported doing so for marketing and advertising.

As AI use is becoming more commonplace, labor leaders and advocates have called for guardrails and regulations to protect workers and consumers, and protections in collective bargaining agreements to ensure workers have a say in AI use and implementation in their workplaces.

“Without proper guardrails, AI systems have supercharged surveillance for both consumers and for the workers who make it possible for consumers to buy what they need or what they want for their loved ones for the holiday season,” said Crystal Weise, policy & programs director at the AFL-CIO Tech Institute, a non-profit labor hub started by the AFL-CIO, the largest federation of unions in the US.

Weise noted surveillance of workers starts at the factories and warehouses where consumer goods are manufactured and distributed, to surveillance of consumers online and in stores, who have their shopping habits tracked and influenced by algorithms, and of workers, with these surveillance systems fueled by AI.

“We know that these surveillance technologies make jobs worse, and we know that it makes products and services more expensive. We need policies and collective bargaining agreements that stop exploitative surveillance,” she added. “We want to see humans in control of how shoppers and consumers are accessing the goods and services that they need.”

Weise said AI-fueled surveillance systems such as surveillance pricing, productivity quotas on workers, and monitoring dissent and workplace organizing efforts are already collecting reams of valuable data on workers and consumers, which is used to cut costs and drive up profit margins.

Shoppers may be subjected to AI before they even walk into a brick-and-mortar store, with several major retailers such as Macy’s, Target, Home Depot and Costco using automated license plate readers (ALPRs), and other retailers using AI tools to scale back Black Friday discounts and bolster their profit margins.

“We use this technology for limited, authorized purposes. Data is collected through ALPRs to prevent theft and fraud, help ensure security, and maintain the safety of individuals and our properties,” states Macy’s disclaimer notice on the use of the technology at some stores.

For workers, they may be subjected to AI from the beginning of applying for a job, such as at Amazon-owned Whole Foods, which uses an AI recruiting agent named Sage – the only way to apply for a job at the company, according to Whole Foods’ website on job applications.

Once in stores, customers and workers can be subjected to AI facial recognition technology, with major retailers such as Wegmans, Macy’s and Home Depot citing use of the technology, and customers are having their data collected by major retailers, such as Kroger, which archives data it collects on customers and sells it, according to a 2025 Consumer Reports investigation.

“We’re not anti-technology, but we are anti-dehumanization of the workplace,” said Stuart Appelbaum, president of the Retail, Wholesale, and Department Store Union and executive vice-president of the United Food and Commercial Workers.

Appelbaum argued AI can’t measure or be aware of life situations that should be accounted for in decisions related to discipline or job termination, and cited negative effects of algorithmic surveillance on workers.

“We’ve seen a rise in algorithmic surveillance, and it creates a pressure cooker environment. People are afraid to pause for a breath, or even to go to the bathroom, and for us, that’s really workplace harassment by algorithm,” he said. “Every worker deserves to have a human involved before any discipline takes place.”

He cited contracts the union has won at employers that include protections on how AI is used and implemented in workplaces, and emphasized the importance of being able to bargain over new technologies as employers are frequently using AI to try to lower labor costs and increase profit margins.

“A lot of retailers are using AI as an excuse to have fewer people on the shop floor,” Appelbaum added. “What you end up doing is diminishing the in-store experience, and I think that’s a huge mistake. Not only does it put pressure on the people who remain working, but it also, I think, isn’t good for the future of the store. Basically, we think the technology should be used to empower and strengthen retail workers, and I think that’s part and parcel of everything we negotiate.”

Fears of large-scale layoffs in the retail industry thanks to AI have yet to materialize. According to a July 2026 policy brief published by Stanford University researchers, AI’s impact on overall employment is “likely small” at the moment. But several firms have announced planned job cuts over the next few years, citing AI or AI investments as a leading factor, and new technologies, such as electronic shelf labels, are projected to result in job losses and increase prices for consumers.

In October 2026, Kroger announced plans to cut 3,000 corporate jobs over the next three years, citing the use of artificial intelligence to streamline operations.

“These notifications are part of the corporate headcount reduction the company announced in early October to lower prices and improve the shopping experience by simplifying operations and better use of technology,” said a Kroger spokesperson on the cuts.

The announcement came after the company was hit with a charge of $2.6bn in 2025 following its decision to shut down three automated robotic delivery centers, which Kroger did not comment on.

“As retailers feel the pressure from Wall Street to cut costs and pump up share prices, they’re turning to AI to do the dirty work,” said Milton Jones, international president of the United Food and Commercial Workers, which represents workers at around two-thirds of Kroger stores in the US. “Whether it’s AI-powered scheduling that slashes retail workers’ hours or surveillance pricing that raises costs for consumers, people are getting squeezed on both sides of the cash register.”

Bryan Wynn, national bargaining director for the United Food and Commercial Workers, said that investors are pushing for artificial intelligence investments at firms to cut labor costs, increase efficiencies, boost profits, largely without concerns for how these technologies affected workers and consumers.

He explained planning for these technologies has exceedingly become a concern in bargaining contract renewals and future union contracts, as retail employers are using AI for data collection and surveillance to influence and monitor the behaviors of workers and consumers, and to use that data to further increase profits.

“People should have a say in how AI and their data are used to change how they work and shop,” added Jones. “We need technology that works for our members, and all working people, not automation that steals their livelihoods.”

FinanceTab.title: Amazon’s sale deals deceive customers, thinktank alleges
FinanceTab.text:
An Apple Watch on sale for $680. A pair of women’s Hunter yellow rainboots discounted for $127, and a pair of men’s UGG boots, $180. A Carhartt beanie just shy of $20.

These discounts – all reportedly featured last year on Amazon’s own curation of its best Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals – sound like good deals for the holiday gift season. But a recent analysis from progressive thinktank Groundwork Collaborative found these products and others had been listed at the same price or even less just days before Amazon started advertising them as discounted.

Overall, researchers found that about 30% of the products Amazon highlighted for its Black Friday and Cyber Monday campaigns were priced the same or even lower in the month before the sale. That share increased to 60% when extending the timeline to 60 days prior to the sale events. Across the board, median sale prices were actually nearly 20% higher than their pre-Black Friday offering.

Those Hunter rainboots, for example, were listed for nearly $50 less – about $80 – just nine days before going on its advertised “sale” Groundwork said. The Apple Watch and men’s UGG boots were both listed for roughly $80 less within a month of the Amazon’s Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales of last year.

It was the “most rigorous, intensive project” that the thinktank had taken on in its history, Lindsay Owens, the president and chief executive of Groundwork, said after the report’s release.

“Americans are really squeezed right now. Back-to-school shopping was expensive. Buying a Thanksgiving meal for your family is going to be expensive. Holiday gift shopping is going to be really expensive,” Owens said in an interview with the Guardian. “Sale events are a really important way that families stretch their dollars, and Americans trust that these Amazon sales events and other sales events around Black Friday and Cyber Monday are worth waiting for, and offer them genuine savings.

“Our report suggests otherwise,” she continued, “that the sale events aren’t always what they’re cracked up to be.”

Amazon said in a statement on its website that the Groundwork Collaborative published “deeply flawed and false claims” and that it “cherrypicked” findings.

“This is the second attempt that Groundwork has made in the past week to assert false claims about our deal events based on flawed methodology and inaccurate data, and it’s clear they have no interest in the facts and are focused on pursuing a pre-determined narrative,” said in the statement.

In further statements to the Guardian, Amazon said that it analyzed deals from the report’s claims and found that 98% of the products in 2024 and 99% of products in 2024 were at the same price or lower over the past 30 days from the sale events.

“When we looked at the research’s actual deals for 2025, we found that 89% of the products had lower prices and 10% were the same, compared with the prior 30-day low prices,” the company said. “Groundwork’s research appears to focus on two low-trafficked corporate blog pages that inadvertently listed some products as deals and was clearly marked as subject to change. Groundwork is basing this misleading claim on a handful of these products that were mistakenly included on those pages but were not badged as deals in our store.”

For products that were accurately labeled as deals, consumers saved an average of more than 35% off list price, the company said.

The report comes as Americans say they are facing higher prices across the board, especially for gas and groceries. Companies have also come under increased scrutiny over unfair pricing practices, including dynamic and surveillance pricing, which Owen has further scrutinized in her recent book, Gouged.

Other governments have made efforts to crack down on unfair pricing practices, especially during Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals. Earlier this month, the European Commission proposed a new ban to regulate certain practices such as on “dark pattern” marketing tactics that falsely claim a product is almost sold out to pressure consumers into purchasing the item. The proposal, which is now under review by the European parliament and council, also threatens companies with fines if they push consumers to buy more or target minors with personalized advertising.

“It’s time for Congress to put Amazon executives in the hot seat and make them come clean about their pricing games,” Elizabeth Pancotti, the Groundwork Collaborative’s vice-president of policy, advocacy and research, said in a news conference after the report was released last week. “And the [Federal Trade Commission] should not wait to resume enforcement of its deceptive pricing guide, which has laid dormant for 50 years, and issue formal rule-making with real teeth.”

FinanceTab.title: China reserves right to take ‘necessary measures’ after Trump’s new tariff proposals
FinanceTab.text:
Beijing has said it reserves the right to take “necessary measures” after Donald Trump’s administration proposed new tariffs on goods from China and other major trading partners, triggering a global backlash.

Among the suggested levies on 14 major trading partners announced on Wednesday, China is potentially facing one of the biggest hits. It would face the highest capped rate of 20%, which in some cases will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45%.

“China urges the United States to correct its erroneous practices and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue and consultation,” the Chinese commerce ministry spokesman, He Yadong, said at a regular briefing. “China will closely monitor developments and reserves the right to take necessary measures to firmly defend its legitimate rights and interests.”

Brazil was also singled out in the announcement after trade talks stalled.

Brazil’s government said on Wednesday that “Brazil will not yield to this type of threat”, adding in its statement that the “unilateral decision constitutes an unacceptable action within the framework of the ongoing bilateral negotiating process”.

It voiced particular indignation at US proposals for higher import taxes for raw and refined sugar and a new 10% tariff on aircraft, a change that would hit Embraer, Brazil’s largest aircraft maker.

It added that Brazil would continue to negotiate “without ruling out the possibility of adopting retaliatory measures in response to the illegal and unjust imposition of tariffs on Brazilian products”.

The Trump administration said that the new tariffs would be consistent with trade deals that the US reached last year with dozens of countries. They are being imposed under a law that allowed the president to target countries the US had found to engage in unreasonable or discriminatory trade practices. Jamieson Greer, the US trade representative, told CNBC that many US trading partners had adopted “market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favour while eroding America’s manufacturing base”.

The Trump administration’s new tariff rates would be capped at lower ​levels ‌agreed under ​trade deals ​that have already been concluded or remain under negotiation.

The administration will seek feedback from affected industries and hold a hearing on 25 January, suggesting the final duties won’t take effect until February or March.

Trump met his counterpart, Xi Jinping, in Shenzhen last week but the escalation in tariffs will not be a surprise to China, Dan Wang, a director on Eurasia Group’s China team, told AFP news agency.

The US and China last year reached a trade truce but that is set to expire on 10 January 2027. Trump and Xi are expected to meet again in Miami on the sidelines of the G20 in December.

“It has become a pattern before every major top leader summit,” Wang said, adding that she did not think the new measures would derail relations between Washington and Beijing.

“Xi has a high incentive to keep bilateral relations stable leading up to the 21st (Communist) party congress in October 2027,”Wang said.

A spokesperson for China’s embassy in Washington rejected allegations that China was ‌a source of ⁠excess capacity.

“The so-called issue of ‘industrial overcapacity’ does not really exist and should not be used as a pretext for political manipulation,” the spokesperson said, urging the two sides to jointly deliver on agreements secured between Trump andd Xi.

Earlier, China’s foreign ministry restated its opposition while calling for the US to resolve the issue through dialogue. “A tariff war or a trade war serves no party’s interests,” said the spokesperson Guo Jiakun.

Greer told CNBC that the administration was proposing a “broad exemption” for $30bn worth of Chinese goods in line with the deal. “We’ve talked to our trading partners about this – they know what we’re proposing,” Greer said. “I think a lot of this is baked in.”

Some US analysts criticised the duties as too weak to change China’s trade practices.

China “is a bigger source of excess production than the rest of the world combined”, said Derek Scissors, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute. Yet Wednesday’s proposal “barely raises existing tariffs on China and will make no difference to the country’s trade behaviour.”

The EU said it rejected the premise of new tariffs and expected the US to stick by a deal struck last year. “The EU and the US share a real concern about global overcapacity, much of it state-driven and concentrated in third countries. We regret the lack of joint action,” said the European Commission spokesperson Olof Gill.

Vietnam’s trade ministry said it was ⁠working with the US to complete its trade deal as soon ⁠as possible and would coordinate with relevant US agencies.

It added it was “preparing ​and submitting ​rebuttal comments on the ​preliminary findings as well as on inaccurate submissions ​and allegations ‌made by ​interested ​parties”.

In response to the US announcement, the Indian government denied it had any structural excess capacity in ⁠any sector, ⁠adding that it remained committed to an early conclusion of ⁠a trade deal between the two countries. Greer has said the tariff ⁠on Indian imports would be capped at 17% if a trade deal was struck.

Taiwan was also earmarked for new tariffs but Taipei on Thursday said it was confident it would keep its existing ⁠15% tariff rate.

Taipei and Washington signed trade deals in January and February of ‌this year, which secured preferential treatment for semiconductors and other tech products that account for ​more than 70% of Taiwan’s exports to the US.

Other countries and regions affected by the new tariffs include Bangladesh, ‌Cambodia, the EU, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland and Thailand.

Tokyo’s top government spokesperson, Minoru Kihara, said it was “regrettable that a proposed measure targeting Japan has been announced”.

Singapore’s government said it was “very disappointed” with the proposals and denied it was protecting its domestic market or subsidising manufacturing.

Trump’s latest round of tariffs may be here to stay despite the Democrats’ electoral sweep in the US midterms. Some Democrats will probably support some of the tariffs, particularly on China. Trump can veto any legislation that seeks to overturn the import taxes.

However, the Democratic senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, who will take over the finance committee next year, said he would “use every tool at my disposal to end Trump’s tariffs chaos”.

He added: “This is another blatant attempt by Donald Trump to reconstruct his illegal global tariffs. Global overcapacity is a serious problem, but Trump’s unilateral price-hiking tariffs are not the solution.”

With Associated Press and Reuters

SportsTab.title: England v New Zealand: Nations Championship game chance for All Blacks to arrest decline
SportsTab.text:
For decades, the All Blacks have defied gravity.

Despite a population, player pool and bank balance smaller than most of their rivals, New Zealand's rugby team have become sporting shorthand for success.

Deservedly so. No other team comes close to them.

England beat the All Blacks this year and last. They play them again on Saturday aiming for a hat-trick.

But, England would need that winning streak to continue until around 2050 just to level up a lop-sided historical head-to-head.

New Zealand have won 36 times to England's 10 in their 121-year rivalry.

For every other nation in Test rugby, the story is the same. New Zealand have the superior record against them all.

A section on the All Blacks' website, titled Rivalries,, external opens by listing South Africa's 40% winning record in their meetings. And the numbers only drop from there.

But New Zealand's grip on the global game appears looser now than ever.

If they lose to England on Saturday, it may not much sway the historical balance between the two teams.

But it would be a sixth defeat in a calendar year, a total matched only once before in the All Blacks past, back in 1949 when a split squad played two Test series in Australia and apartheid South Africa at the same time.

This current crop of All Blacks are suffering not just by comparison to the previous generation, but when set against every other modern predecessor.

One reason may be a source of strength turning against them.

The All Blacks' culture of promoting within and establishing coaching dynasties was seen as key when they were winning.

A thread ran through the Graham Henry, Steve Hansen and Ian Foster succession in the 2010s glory days. The latter two served under their predecessor and the first two earned their Test stripes with Wales, before taking the top job.

All were schooled as coaches in New Zealand and steeped in the country's rugby traditions.

The in-house production line of leaders ensured continuity and protected a team ethos that has been admired and written about everywhere.

But, in a modern world in which opposition tactics are quickly picked apart and best practice spreads fast, has adherence to tradition held back the team?

New Zealand's rivals have all hired coaching talent from outside.

Rassie Erasmus, South African to the core, may front the Springbok coaching operation, but behind him Irishmen Jerry Flannery and Felix Jones and Tony Brown, a former All Black himself, bring specialist knowledge to different areas.

France, famously patriotic in their hiring, benefited from Englishman Shaun Edwards and South African Vlok Cilliers' work behind the scenes in recent years.

England, Ireland, Scotland and Wales all have or have had head coaches from other countries.

Dave Rennie, who has coached Australia, Glasgow Warriors and Japanese side Kobe Steelers previously, became the first person of Pasifika heritage to lead the All Blacks when he took on the job in March.

He has brought a Scottish contingent to mix up his backroom, with attack coach Mike Blair the most high-profile.

But his regime is still only eight months old. Other issues predate it.

Most pressing is the balance sheet.

New Zealand Rugby is leaking millions. A failure to balance the books means it has built-in annual losses of about NZ$20m (£8.35m), and is projected to lose NZ$66m (£27.6m) between 2027 and 2031., external

The All Black brand is valuable. It has been licensed to sell watches, healthcare and information technology.

The team are still a powerful global draw.

They are among the keenest Test nations to play matches overseas, where they can fill stadiums bigger than Auckland's 50,000-capacity Eden Park and make more money.

A globe-trotting 2026 itinerary has filled coffers, but emptied players.

Still though costs are rising faster than their income.

In turn, that is compromising the All Blacks' ability to keep their centrally contracted stars at home.

As in England, playing for a domestic team is a requirement to play internationally.

Thirty-five-year-old playmaker Beauden Barrett's proposed move to Bristol Bears and out of eligibility at the end of the 2027 Rugby World Cup attracted headlines, but New Zealand are more concerned by other departures.

Back-row star Wallace Sititi, 24, is rumoured to have agreed a move to Stade Francais, while Luke Jacobson, 29, has already announced his own switch to fellow French side Bayonne.

"What bothers us is when All Blacks or highly prospective All Blacks leave in their sort of mid-20s," said New Zealand Rugby chairman and World Cup-winning captain David Kirk this week., external

"When they want to go away for two or three years or something like that in their mid-20s, possibly come back, but possibly not come back. That's a problem for us.

"We're not ever going to win on the money. We just don't have the money to compete with Japan and France, who are the two big payers.

"So we have to compete on the desire to play for the All Blacks and to have a career that's memorable representing New Zealand. And most of the time that's absolutely fine.

"That's why the few people leaving become a bit of a cause célèbre - because not many do."

Richie Mo'unga is one of them.

He was New Zealand's first-choice fly-half at the last World Cup and arguably the best in the position in the world.

He spent three years in Japanese club rugby and international exile afterwards, and has yet to fully find his feet on his return.

New Zealand have the talent to cope. Ruben Love is a coming force at 10. Many of their stars will time stints overseas around World Cups. But it robs them of options and makes cohesion and succession trickier.

Sabbaticals – approved overseas stints which allow players to take up short, lucrative stints at overseas clubs and remain available for the All Blacks – have been a compromise.

Ardie Savea, talismanic All Blacks captain, has been playing in Japan on one this season.

But, overseas clubs hungry for Kiwi talent on a longer-term basis are circling.

There is another angle to the issue that cuts against the All Blacks.

Those who do stay and remain eligible are competing in a weakened Super Rugby tournament.

South African sides left in 2020, throwing their lot in with the United Rugby Championship and the European club scene.

With only Australian sides and the Fijian Drua to compete against, Kiwi provincial sides' fixture lists are a significant step down from international rugby.

It is far from ideal preparation for the Test arena.

Then add in the cross-code lure.

New Zealand Warriors, the Auckland-based NRL side, offer a convenient and potentially lucrative route into the 13-man game for young rugby talent.

After taking a hit during Covid, grassroots rugby league numbers have ticked upwards., external Rugby union's equivalent numbers have been propped up by a rise in women's participation.

For the all-conquering All Blacks, suddenly the problems are stacking up.

Win or lose against England, they and New Zealand Rugby know they are playing a longer game. One they cannot afford to lose.

SportsTab.title: Qatar Grand Prix 2026: Antonelli tops second practice as Gasly crashes
SportsTab.text:
World champion Kimi Antonelli set the pace ahead of Mercedes team-mate George Russell in a disrupted second practice at the Qatar Grand Prix.

Italian Antonelli was 0.127 seconds quicker than Russell on the medium tyre, as neither driver set a time on the soft compound because of two red flags that punctuated the session.

Lewis Hamilton also came to halt after his Ferrari lost power, with a virtual safety car deployed so the marshals could come to the seven-time world champion's aid.

The McLarens of Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri plus Red Bull's Max Verstappen completed the top five at the Lusail International Circuit, with the trio setting soft-tyre times that were more than four tenths adrift of the two Mercedes.

The first red flag was to clear gravel off the track after an incident for Ferrari's Charles Leclerc early on, while the other was to recover the Alpine of Pierre Gasly following a high-speed spin.

Frenchman Gasly hit a marker board before beaching himself after taking too much kerb at Turn 14 in the middle of the qualifying simulation runs.

The interruptions led to the second hour being extended by 13 minutes to allow drivers more time on track in the representative conditions.

"It was a productive day," said Antonelli. "We tried a lot of things on the car between FP1 and FP2, but in FP2, it seemed like we did a step back with the car.

"But it was very interesting to see how the car behaved after those changes. It's not easy."

Antonelli, who secured his maiden title in Mexico City earlier this month, was also fastest in the opening session on the mediums. Mercedes did fit the 20-year-old with the soft tyre in the first hour, but he failed to set a lap time on them.

He said he feels it will be close between himself and Russell for the race victory, but added: "You can never write off Max [Verstappen] and the others."

Norris, meanwhile, said Mercedes "were in a different category" to McLaren, highlighting the Silver Arrows "were quicker in every single corner by miles".

The 2025 world champion added: "We seem in a relatively decent position, similar on pace with Red Bull, and similar-ish to Ferrari. So I'd say it's OK."

Four-time title winner Verstappen said it had been a "difficult day" following his issues with heavy steering towards the end of the session.

"The balance of the car is probably too disconnected at the moment to go fast," he added. "It's costing us quite a bit of lap time."

Hamilton also had a moment with Verstappen that was noted by the race control. The Briton was on a flying lap when he got too close to the Dutchman, who was on a long run.

Verstappen said Hamilton had moved under braking, but the stewards decided no further investigation was needed.

The second Red Bull of Isack Hadjar was sixth on the timesheets, with Leclerc leading Hamilton in seventh and eighth, 1.3 seconds away from Antonelli's time.

The two Racing Bulls of British rookie Arvid Lindblad and Liam Lawson were ninth and 10th.

Leclerc had to head back into the garage after spinning and going through the gravel when Lawson was just ahead of him at Turn Nine.

The Monegasque driver said the car did not feel right, and the Italian team spent a chunk of time repairing the damage to the floor. After the session he said he lost control after going a little bit early on the throttle.

Ferrari arrived in Qatar after another on-track incident between Leclerc and Hamilton, this time in Las Vegas. The pair made contact and Leclerc was given a 10-second penalty for the incident, with Hamilton saying on Thursday the team were facing "very, very challenging times".

Leclerc thinks this weekend could potentially be another struggle for the Italian team, who can secure second in the constructors' championship if they can retain at least a 44-point lead over third-placed Red Bull.

"A very, very difficult day. Not even on high fuel were we strong," said Leclerc.

"We are working hard but for some reason, Mercedes is so much faster than I think everyone expected. So the gaps are just a little bit strange."

Drivers will be limited to a maximum of 27 laps on a set of tyres at the Lusail circuit, meaning teams will have to make at least two pit stops during the 57-lap grand prix on Sunday, which starts at 16:00 GMT.

The decision is caused by concern over the integrity of the Pirelli tyres on the high-speed, 16-corner track. Laps to the grid, formation laps and any laps completed after the end of the race will not be included.

Hamilton was told by his engineer in first practice tyre degradation was "much higher than expected" after highlighting his own issues.

Qatar and next week's finale in Abu Dhabi are going ahead as planned despite the ongoing conflict between the United States/Israel and Iran.
