articles.title: Wales v Japan: Steve Tandy’s side aim to finish Nations Championship campaign with flourish
articles.text:
It is not the traditional ending to a Wales rugby autumn campaign.

After the euphoria and then disappointment of two epic international weekends in Cardiff, Wales face the prospect of finishing a November series in south west London with a fixture against Japan.

It sounds unusual because the conclusion of the inaugural Nations Championship is exactly that.

The concept of a finals weekend in one venue with six games over three days is laudable, but trying to get Welsh fans excited about defeating Japan to finish ninth rather than 10th in a 12-team tournament at a neutral ground is a tough sell, especially when you compare it to what happened in Cardiff two weeks ago.

This autumn will always be remembered as the campaign where Wales shocked the rugby world by beating New Zealand for the first time since 1953.

Either side of that momentous day, there has been a lacklustre 28-21 defeat of Japan and a narrow 29-26 loss against Australia in a game Wales could and maybe should have won.

Those exciting occasions in Cardiff will now be followed by a trip to Twickenham to take on Eddie Jones' Japan. It takes some getting used to.

It will be a strange experience with Wales facing Japan on a Saturday afternoon before England play New Zealand for third place.

Is it a double-header or will Wales be providing the curtain-raiser to the main event?

Whichever way you view the occasion, Wales head coach Steve Tandy knows his side will have to provide their own atmosphere with a sparse crowd present for Friday afternoon's match between Italy and Fiji before Ireland took on Australia in the evening.

"We've spoken about it all week," said Tandy.

"There's also a 40-minute bus trip which is not normal either because we usually stay closer.

"We have also spoken about it being an early kick-off.

"There might be people walking in while the game is going on, the crowd might fill up as the game goes on, so there's all these little things to consider.”

Tandy says the squad know Twickenham will not match the intensity of Cardiff's Principality Stadium during the past couple of weeks.

"It is a different type of atmosphere for us after three massive games at home and being unbelievably well supported," said Tandy.

"We've got to adapt a different sort of mindset and create that energy on the field for ourselves."

Wales finished fifth in the northern hemisphere table of the inaugural Nations Championship to face Japan, who finished in the same position in the southern standings.

It will be the fifth time in 16 months the two sides have faced each other, with Wales winning three out of the four games.

So opposing coaches Tandy and Jones will again lock horns.

"I am looking forward to seeing him once more but it is probably a little bit too much," said Tandy, who saw his side labour to an 28-21 win over Japan three weeks ago.

Since that result, Japan have suffered a 78-15 hammering by England and a 67-5 drubbing by Scotland.

"We can't be fooled by the scoreboards, Japan have still got the core of their forward pack and line-out pressure," said Tandy.

"We're going to have to produce one of our best performances of the tournament to make sure we finish the campaign the way we want to."

Japan are down to their bare bones after a hard programme they are not used to, but Jones remains bullish.

"It should be good, a great occasion," said Jones.

"Wales don't like coming to Twickenham and for us, it's a great experience, so we will give it a red-hot crack."

Fighting words, but this is a chance for Wales to produce the type of commanding performance and victory that has been missing against this opposition.

Wales' three victories in the past four games against Japan have been by nine, seven and one point.

Given Tandy's selection this week and Japan's exertions in recent weeks, a commanding win should be on the agenda to match Scotland and England’s exploits against the Brave Blossoms.

Nothing defines a Welsh rugby nation like differing viewpoints of the make-up of a national team, with the old adage of Wales having three million selectors.

Tandy’s opinion is the only one that counts but he has had plenty of contrasting advice from the Welsh public this week.

In one corner, you have somebody like former Wales wing Alex Cuthbert stating on the Scrum V podcast that Tandy should have selected a full side to put Japan to the sword and build momentum towards next year's Six Nations.

Then you open up social media, with the vocal element telling the Wales head coach he should be blooding more players.

Tandy has made five changes from the side that lost to Australia with seven players - full-back Blair Murray, wing Louis Rees-Zammit, centres Eddie James and Max Llewellyn, fly-half Sam Costelow, prop Archie Griffin and lock Dafydd Jenkins - starting all four matches in the November campaign.

Uncapped quartet Che Hope, Macs Page, Rhys Barratt and Aneurin Owen are among the players who have not been given game time, alongside Liam Belcher, Tom Rogers, Seb Davies, Keiron Assiratti and Jarrod Evans.

It is the first time Wales have not blooded a new cap in an autumn campaign this century.

"It wasn't deliberate," said Tandy.

"We've handed out probably roughly nine new caps over the last couple of campaigns.

"We feel we have got a young group that are growing and we want to keep our cohesion while freshening things up.

"We are starting to probably see the spine of our team developing and our squad becoming more consistent.

"When we're picking the team, it's about performance and we've also got one eye on the future.

"We felt this is the right sort of blend to go and produce a performance on the weekend."

Tandy knows there will be a number of disappointed players returning to their clubs after their lack of match opportunities during the past month.

"What the group spoke about on the first Sunday that we came back in, is that we've got to be competitive right across the board," said Tandy.

"You're going to have disappointed players and you can't keep everyone happy, because they all want an opportunity.

"International rugby is tough and we need to have competition."

Wherever the location of the final match of the year and the make-up of the side, the mood music currently surrounding the Welsh men’s national side is significantly more uplifting than it was 12 months ago.

Tandy's first autumn in charge in 2025 was a testing one, with a one-point win against Japan overshadowed by three heavy defeats against Argentina, New Zealand and South Africa, who inflicted a 73-0 hammering in the final game.

In contrast, Wales are chasing a third win this November with a double against Japan either side of that first famous victory against the All Blacks in 73 years, as they look to keep ninth place in the world rankings.

"It has flown by," said Tandy.

"I can't believe how quick the campaign's gone and it's going to finish on Saturday.

"It's been an amazing tournament and we are looking forward to hopefully finishing with a positive performance."

articles.title: Fury vs Joshua: Tyson Fury cleared to fight Anthony Joshua after medical checks
articles.text:
Tyson Fury has been medically cleared to fight Anthony Joshua in December after the bout was put in jeopardy by claims of a schizophrenia diagnosis.

Fury, 38, spoke of his mental health struggles in a Netflix documentary which was released on Friday, with his wife, Paris, saying he had been diagnosed with schizophrenia.

But Paris has since retracted that statement, saying he "doesn't have this condition" and Netflix have edited the remarks out of their film.

The British Boxing Board of Control (BBBoC) told BBC Sport: "Tyson Fury has been cleared to box on 11 December."

Fury faces Joshua, 37, in a long overdue all-British heavyweight contest at Cardiff's Principality Stadium in the early hours of 12 December.

Originally, the Netflix documentary featured the Furys recalling his admission to hospital in June 2016 with a suspected heart attack.

Doctors said he had suffered an anxiety attack. He was diagnosed with schizophrenia after he left hospital, according to the film.

The NHS describes schizophrenia as a form of psychosis, and symptoms can include hallucinations, delusions and muddled thoughts and speech.

Under regulation 8.1(b) of the British Boxing Board of Control's 2026 rules and regulations, schizophrenia is among the conditions that "may preclude" a boxer from obtaining a first licence, while for an existing licence holder the board "may take such action as in its absolute discretion as it sees fit".

On Thursday, the BBBoC general secretary Robert Smith told BBC Sport that it was "in the process of dealing with the matter" and that it was "confident he [Tyson Fury] will be absolutely fine".

Eddie Hearn, who runs Joshua's promoter Matchroom, said he has not watched the documentary but believes the Furys may have unintentionally provided false information.

"I think that Tyson's been through his own battles and sometimes things that he says aren't 100% medically clarified, but he's probably got his own way of explaining things."

Hearn praised the BBBoC for its handling of the situation over the past 24 hours, calling the governing body one of the "best commissions in the world".

"If there was any situation where anyone was diagnosed with that and coming into a fight then there is no way the board would let him fight, so that's definitely not the case," he added.

"I think the board would ask for clarification of that. Everyone has to go through an examination anyway. I would think he would be assessed, cleared and ready to fight."

articles.title: Arsenal vs Man City: What can Enzo Maresca's side learn from defensively strong Gunners?
articles.text:
Manchester City's leaky defence faces one of its most difficult tasks of the season with a trip to watertight Arsenal, aiming to put right their patchy recent form.

Enzo Maresca's side began the season with eight straight victories but have won only one of their past seven in all competitions inside 90 minutes and head to Emirates Stadium trailing the champions by six points even at this early juncture.

A Premier League defeat on Sunday could well have long-term consequences for City's title aspirations, with Mikel Arteta's men clearly standing above any other top-flight side as the ones to topple.

Though the Gunners dropped points last weekend with a draw at Newcastle, they continue to set the standards with a miserly defence that has conceded only seven goals in the club's opening 11 league games.

Asked why he felt City have dropped off in recent weeks, Maresca - who replaced Pep Guardiola as manager in the summer - said: "For me it's because we've had four months together. Transition requires time.

"It's probably because we won seven games in a row, with Champions League eight in a row. Everyone was thinking at City there's no transition but I've said many times I am not a magician. There is transition, it's normal.

"There are eight or nine new players, the manager is new so you need time and you can see different clubs when they had transition how complicated it is. For me, it's completely normal, I'm completely relaxed, no panic at all."

"We are conceding too many goals and we need to avoid that," was an obvious statement made by Maresca following last Saturday's 1-1 draw against Fulham.

City followed that up with another home stalemate against Napoli in the Champions League on Tuesday and have now conceded in 10 successive games in all competitions for the first time in seven years.

"[It was] far, far too easy to play through [City]," said former England captain Alan Shearer of Rodrigo Muniz's goal for Fulham on Match of the Day.

"Fulham's throw-in was level with their own 18-yard box. For them to get through is not acceptable at any level, let alone when you are playing for Manchester City and Muniz ran past the entire midfield [to score]."

City have managed only five clean sheets all campaign, which is in stark contrast to Arsenal, who have kept double the amount so far, while Newcastle's opening goal ended a run off 445 minutes without the ball hitting their net.

Maresca's men also have an issue by conceding the opener, having done so seven times in the past 10 games, and of the 14 goals they have shipped, six have come inside the first 20 minutes.

An early Arsenal goal may well be an important factor in deciding Sunday's contest.

Asked how his side can improve defensively, Maresca said: "Video [analysis], meetings, [on] pitch coaching, It is a mix of that.

"Some of the goals we concede we can avoid, so hopefully we can do that."

The injury to key defender William Saliba has almost gone unnoticed for Arsenal as Ezri Konsa has stepped in to fill the void at centre-back seamlessly since joining from Aston Villa in the summer.

The England international has established a formidable partnership with Gabriel and the two have quickly formed an impressive understanding this season.

Maresca, meanwhile, admitted he was still "trying to find different" solutions to his team, which has been highlighted by the chopping and changing of his backline.

In 16 Premier League and Champions League games this season, the Italian has used eight different combinations in defence, which has given players little chance of fostering any sort of on-pitch relationships with each other.

City have also made seven errors leading to goals, compared to Arsenal's one.

"You are concerned in some way because that is a lot of errors leading to goals," said former City defender Nedum Onuoha. "With some of the best players you ask, 'what are they really good at?' For some it is the fact they don't make mistakes.

"They are ruthless and relentless in the way they play but at this moment in time City are being punished for those errors.

"A manager can have the tactics and do the team talks, but if people are going to continue to make those mistakes, they will suffer."

The chant of "1-0 to the Arsenal" has been synonymous with the Gunners over the years and it could not be more apt under Arteta.

Since the start of last season, his side have won 16 matches in all competitions by that particular scoreline, compared to six by City.

After beating Sunderland in a chaotic match in September, Maresca said he would "prefer to win 1-0 than 5-3", suggesting his side needed more control and he re-iterated that message after the Fulham draw.

"Sometimes you need to win games 1-0 for a small difference and to keep a clean sheet but in this moment we are not able to do that," he admitted.

City, though, have scored five more league goals than Arsenal in this campaign and Sunday's hosts have injury concerns over goalkeeper David Raya.

The Spaniard is a doubt with the shoulder problem he picked up at Newcastle, and compatriot Kepa Arrizabalaga may deputise again as he did in the 1-1 draw against Borussia Dortmund in the Champions League on Tuesday.

City have fond memories of coming up against Arsenal's stand-in keeper, after Kepa's howler for the opening goal contributed to their 2-0 Carabao Cup final triumph back in March.

A repeat result on Sunday will provide a much-needed morale boost for Maresca and his team.

articles.title: Nathan Lyon: Australia set to drop off-spinner for first New Zealand Test
articles.text:
Australia are set to drop off-spinner Nathan Lyon for the first Test against New Zealand, with uncapped Corey Rocchiccioli expected to be named in the squad.

The omission of Lyon for the Test in Perth from 9-13 December is not thought to be linked to the sandpaper controversy.

Lyon was part of the Australia XI in Cape Town in 2018 and, three years later, joined his fellow bowlers in releasing a statement denying involvement in the cheating plot.

Lyon has not spoken publicly since the debate over the sandpaper saga re-emerged with the allegation raised in former batter Usman Khawaja's autobiography that the entire team knew about the ball-tampering.

The decision to omit Lyon, a mainstay of their team for 15 years, is a significant move by Australia and leaves the 39-year-old's international career at a crossroads.

With 577 Test wickets, Lyon is sixth on the all-time list, with more wickets than any Australian apart from the legendary Shane Warne. In terms of off-spinners, only Sri Lanka great Muttiah Muralitharan has more.

But Lyon has struggled with form and fitness ever since hobbling out of the second Ashes Test at Lord's in 2023 with a calf injury.

In the most recent Ashes series of 2025-26, Lyon did not bowl a ball in the first Test in Perth, was left out of the day-night Test in Brisbane, then sustained a series-ending injury in the third Test in Adelaide.

Whereas the omission of Lyon would once have been unthinkable, Australia have recently left him out of their XI on a regular basis in order play an extra seamer.

Lyon has repeatedly stated his desire to extend his career in order to win Test series away in India and England - challenges Australia face in 2027.

He may still be required on the spin-friendly pitches of India, but 29-year-old Rocchiciolli now has the opportunity to be become Australia's number one.

Also an off-spinner, Rocchiciolli offers Australia the option of batting depth - he made 140 for Western Australia against Tasmania in the Sheffield Shield earlier this week.

Australia host New Zealand for four Tests in December and January.

articles.title: Jamal Musiala: What next for Bayern Munich star?
articles.text:
Bayern Munich - and representatives of one of their most prominent players - have collided over recent weeks.

During the summer, the public became aware that their star 23-year-old midfielder Jamal Musiala suffered from absence seizures.

This neurological condition causes a brief, sudden lapse in awareness and responsiveness. Musiala had two of these lapses during pre-season games, but episodes already happened during the previous year.

At first, the shock among fans and observers was huge. Bayern kept Musiala's condition a secret for some time, and only a few insiders knew about it. In the days after Musiala's lapse during a friendly against Heidenheim, speculations arose over whether the player's medical issue had been known before he signed a highly lucrative contract extension in February 2025.

But it has been confirmed by sources close to the team - and Bayern themselves - that the condition had not been detected before April 2025. One source described Musiala, at the time of signing his new contract, as being "in great health".

In April 2025, days after suffering a muscle tear, Musiala caused a high-speed car crash which cost him his driver's licence. Munich's public prosecutor's office responded to a recent enquiry saying there is no evidence that the accident was caused by a lapse, nor that it was the cause of Musiala's condition.

Nevertheless, checks a couple of days after the crash revealed he was suffering from absence seizures. Musiala's camp consulted numerous experts and hired doctors to treat the player, with the knowledge of Jochen Hahne, Bayern's team doctor. How close the consultations between the external doctors and Bayern's medical staff are remains a point of discussion, among many other things in this complex matter.

Soon after, Musiala's football-related injuries became an issue. He broke his fibula and injured his ankle during the Fifa Club World Cup after colliding with then PSG goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma. He needed months to recover and suffered a subsequent ankle injury, likely related to the leg injury.

After the 2026 World Cup he had a metal plate removed from his left foot, which affected his pre-season preparation. Musiala just recently recovered from a weeks-long absence due to a hamstring tear.

However, his comeback lasted just two games - he came off the bench in Bayern's 1-1 Bundesliga draw against Cologne, and in the Champions League defeat by Lille, but the club confirmed on Friday that he has torn his right hamstring and will be out until further notice.

On top of that, new incidents related to his neurological condition have come to light. Days before his recent return to training, Musiala had another lapse, just like he did on the morning of a Champions League game against Real Madrid in April.

All of this is the tragic story of a highly talented footballer who might never return to his previous level and must deal with a medical condition for the rest of his life.

Absence seizures require daily medication. There are other high-level athletes, such as England rugby union player Tommy Freeman, who have had to deal with the same condition.

A controversy erupted last Friday, as Bayern faced Cologne in what was supposed to be an ordinary league game. Karl-Heinz Rummenigge, once chairman of the board and now a member of Bayern's supervisory board, asked a TV crew to come to his section in the stands.

The unscheduled post-game interview unfolded in a way that no-one at Bayern, not even other members of the club's hierarchy, expected.

"He has a health issue, which is known, and it is known that he has a contract which includes hefty sums of money," Rummenigge said. "You need to talk to the family, to the player and most importantly to the agency, because these sums are - with all due respect - not justifiable any longer."

A day later, chairman of the board Jan-Christian Dreesen and club president Herbert Hainer tried to defuse the situation at the yearly membership assembly, but were also attacked by club member Jonathan Hoffmann.

Hoffmann, a neurologist, said it wouldn't help to go after Musiala publicly, for which he received applause from many of the present members.

One might wonder why an experienced deal-maker like Rummenigge would willingly put down one of his players who could still be valuable to the club, even if it's just for a sale.

He might have been agitated by the way the home game against Cologne went. Harry Kane suffered a ligament tear in his ankle early in the game and star winger Michael Olise had to leave the stadium on crutches.

But, even more importantly, it has become clear that Rummenigge was unhappy with how contract negotiations with Musiala's camp - between October 2024 and February 2025 - unfolded.

Bayern and particularly Max Eberl, the club's director of sport, were running out of time, as Musiala's contract would have ended with the conclusion of the 2025-26 season. If they hadn't reached an agreement before April or May 2025, Bayern would have felt obliged to sell Musiala during the summer transfer window.

Musiala played an impressive Euro 2024 for Germany and was one of Bayern's best players during the period of negotiations. Among others, Real Madrid were interested, but only for a free transfer in 2026.

Keep in mind, Musiala has quite a unique profile as a No 10 that can also come from the wing and break down low-block defences with his dribbles and passing.

Under pressure and confronted by a shrewd negotiator in Christian Schmid, Musiala's agent and a trained lawyer, Bayern agreed to a salary package that could earn Musiala, in a best-case scenario, £21m a year, with £15m as a base salary. Bayern also agreed to grant a signing fee of close to £25m, paid over the stretch of the contract. Musiala even got his wish granted of receiving his own box at Allianz Arena.

Some reports indicated that the fact Musiala's deal includes sick pay for six months, in the case of injury or illness, could be interpreted as circumstantial evidence that the player's representatives may have known about his condition beforehand. A standard Bundesliga contract only offers sick pay for six weeks before insurance would shoulder the payments.

But even six months is a short period in comparison. Premier League players receive their full basic wage for the first 18 months. And, when Bayern negotiate with top players, they ultimately compete against Europe's elite.

Rummenigge, and to a lesser extent his long-time boardroom compatriot Uli Hoeness, made Eberl responsible for the unfavourable terms - arguing that Schmid essentially played Eberl.

Eberl has been the target of criticism from the two former powerbrokers for quite some time. At a recent supervisory board meeting, Hoeness is said to have attacked Eberl for his inactivity over the Musiala issue in the past six months.

That being said, Bayern bought into the Musiala hype for a couple of years, hoping that they would have a superstar of their own who could be marketed across the globe.

The relationship between the club and agent Schmid has been strained to say the least, with Rummenigge particularly disliking him. Some sources believe this was one of the root causes for Rummenigge's recent attack on live TV.

When a 16-year-old Kennet Eichhorn came on the market during the summer, as he wanted to leave second-division side Hertha Berlin, Bayern were interested but ultimately dropped out of the race for the highly touted midfielder. Eichhorn is represented by Schmid and ended up joining Bayer Leverkusen.

Hoeness met with Schmid during the summer to discuss how to proceed with Musiala, but the player's agent did not indicate that they would agree to a wage reduction. Hoeness called the matter a "dilemma" for Bayern during a TV show earlier this month, but did not go as far as Rummenigge.

As long as Musiala is not medically forced to retire, he will receive the wage that was agreed upon in February 2025. Even if Bayern would intend to part ways with the player, they would need to do everything in their power to get the player as close to his previous form as possible.

The release clause of £125m, which could be triggered next year, seems unrealistic. Any comments by Bayern bosses against Musiala, or further leaks to the media, may indeed lower his market value down to zero - unless the player can simply shake things off and perform again.

Eberl and head coach Vincent Kompany have come out to back Musiala. Joshua Kimmich, one of Bayern's veteran players, also criticised the treatment of Musiala after a 2-1 loss to Lille in the Champions League on Wednesday. "Of course, the club is above all and bigger than the player, but not bigger than the human. This is an absolute no-go and also not Bayern-like," Kimmich said.

Even football players' union Fifpro condemned Rummenigge's comments. On Wednesday, Bayern put out a statement saying that a meeting between the club and Musiala's representatives took place on Tuesday, in which it was agreed that the player's health should be paramount.

Whether the damage can be repaired is up in the air. As Bayern have a number of attacking players sidelined, they need a healthy and mentally prepared Musiala in the coming weeks and months.

articles.title: DWP 'cyber incident' causes millions to lose access to benefits and pensions services
articles.text:
Millions of people have been left without access to online benefits and pensions services after the government said its system had been hit by a "cyber incident".

Downing Street has not ruled out an attempted hack but said there was "currently no evidence" personal data had been lost, adding an investigation was ongoing.

The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) said it took the digital services down as a "precaution", and assured claimants regular benefit and pension payments would be paid.

But a number of benefits recipients say money they rely on has still not come through - and they fear being penalised for not being able to fill in an online journal that proves they are looking for jobs.

Single Cardiff mother-of-four Samantha Reah told the BBC she was missing £1,600: "I rely on the payment today - it's my payday.

"I have just enough money in my account to do a food shop. I'm panicking - it's going to be a long and stressful weekend."

Georgina Howarth, 30, from Plymouth, said she had to ask her mother for money to help buy food after not receiving her universal credit payment.

"I've been on the phone to them [DWP staff] every hour since 8am. They said they can't even get on the system."

Claimants are also unable to fill in an online journal which shows the DWP they have been applying for jobs, a condition of their benefits.

Gemma Barnes from St Neots in Cambridgeshire told the BBC she was worried her payments could be cut as a result.

She said she has been trying to access the universal credit website "all of today and since last night as well" but she has not been able to get through to the site.

"With it being so close to Christmas I need [that money] at the moment," she said., explaining she has to often rely on items in the reduced food section to make ends meet.

The DWP says regular payments are not affected and if customers have any issues with their payments, they should call on their benefit phoneline. They say they will not be sanctioned over missing journal entries during the incident.

There are also problems with Healthy Start, an NHS scheme for women who are pregnant or have young children to help them buy milk or fruit.

A spokesperson told the BBC the online application service was unavailable but there was no interruption to payments.

The disruption follows several high-profile tech outages in the UK and around the world in recent months.

As of around 12:00 GMT on Friday, the online systems for pensions, universal credit and Pip applications, as well as the "Tell Us Once'" system to inform government when someone has died, could not be accessed.

It was not clear when the government expected services to be up and running again.

A DWP spokesperson said: "We are working closely with the National Cyber Security Centre and Government Cyber Coordination Centre to investigate and to bring services back online as quickly as possible and to minimise any disruption."

A statement continued: "As always, we will never message you to ask for bank details or ask you to click on links."

Tech disruption to major service around the world have hit the headlines repeatedly in recent months.

There was a major outage of Microsoft services, the grounding of all US flights, problems at the US National Security Agency, and disruption at major American banks.

The causes of these incidents have varied. Many were linked to upgrades going wrong but experts have also mentioned factors including outdated IT systems and the use of AI to potentially exploit tech vulnerabilities.

While the nature of the DWP incident is unclear, officials could not rule out the involvement of a "malicious actor", but added there was "no evidence" that other government departments had been targeted in this way.

The DWP outage follows warnings that AI technology could fuel attacks on UK digital infrastructure.

Earlier this month a National Cyber Security Centre report urged organisations to strengthen their defences against hackers as the technology becomes more complex and capable.

Its CEO Richard Horne said there was a "real prospect of an unprecedented rise in the number of cyber incidents".

Last month the government carried out inspections on several websites after a flaw was identified in a programming language used around the world.

The PHP security flaw prompted a global race for organisations to identify whether they were impacted and fix it before it could be exploited.

UK government websites have been impacted by other cyber incidents in recent years.

In April 2025, the government reported that cyber attackers had breached the Legal Aid Agency's online services.

It said the group responsible accessed a "significant amount" of personal data going back decades, including contact details of people who had applied for legal aid.

The agency took some services offline while responding to the incident.

articles.title: Inside the rogue trader networks scamming customers at scale
articles.text:
Organised networks of rogue plumbers and electricians have been scamming people on a large scale, a BBC investigation has found.

Nessar Khawaja, who used the online name ThatGuyNess, regularly posted TikTok videos showing his work as a plumber, explaining how he made thousands of pounds from "desperate" customers, and recruiting online to expand his network.

"Me and my team, we're top of the food chain," he said in one video.

The investigation found the 23-year-old is a key figure within an organised group that is systematically ripping off customers and teaching others to do the same.

The BBC put these allegations to Khawaja in writing. He denied any wrongdoing and said his social media posts were intended as light-hearted comedy that did not reflect how he operated in practice.

In a recorded phone call, Khawaja insisted he was an entertainer, was joking and that the BBC had "taken things out of context".

In another video, Khawaja made claims he had electricians working for him who made more than £40,000 a month.

"I've got 100-120 engineers. Imagine how much money I am making them and making from them," he said.

One of Khawaja's associates told an undercover BBC journalist during a secretly-recorded recruitment call that engineers working for them had to hand over 60% from every job to the network.

After being approached for comment, TikTok said it banned the account for "breaching its rules on fraud and scams".

Trading Standards said the average rogue trader call-out scam now costs the victim about £10,000.

The impact can be devastating.

Clive, who lives in London, is undergoing treatment for cancer.

He said he had felt forced to pay the rogue trader who came to his home and charged £9,153 for installing an outdoor socket to fit garden lights he already owned.

An independent electrical expert told the BBC the job had not been done properly, was left in an unsafe state and should have cost no more than £250.

Clive said he no longer feels safe in his home.

He explained how he had searched for a local electrician on Google when his usual tradesperson was unavailable and came across Chriss Electrician Ltd.

Clive said the engineer spent about two hours at the property before presenting him with the bill.

"I was shocked," said Clive.

He added he had felt pressured into paying as the work had already been completed.

He went to his local bank branch to move money between accounts before returning home and making the payment through the engineer's portable card reader.

Despite his doubts about the costs, Clive said he had feared what might happen if he refused to pay.

"If I hadn't paid him, I thought something might happen," he said.

"When people come to the door now, I think, 'Oh God, who's that?' I don't feel safe any more."

Like Clive, another man, who the BBC has named as Tom, felt he had no choice but to settle the bill when he mistakenly called a rogue trader to his property in Essex after finding a leak.

He says he was initially quoted £49 over the phone after calling a listing at the top of Google purporting to be an established business.

But on arrival, the plumber increased the call-out fee to £250 and the costs kept on climbing.

"He charged us for the first load of repairs, and then the second load with the water cylinder. Basically, he was running my taps constantly saying, 'Look, it's coming out this hot', which caused me to panic."

By the end, the plumber presented a bill for £6,237.60.

"I noticed afterwards that the invoice said Ibby & Co. Ltd. That was when alarm bells started ringing because I had never heard of that company. It wasn't the company I called out, essentially."

Tom called another plumber to get a second opinion and was told the work that was completed should have cost no more than £1,000.

When Tom called the company to complain, he received threats from an unknown man. The call was recorded and the BBC heard threats including: "We'll show up at your house. And we're gonna be sleeping there for months."

Ibrahim Nazir, the plumber who came to Tom's property and the listed director of Ibby and Co Ltd, has been contacted by the BBC for comment but has not responded.

Sources close to Khawaja place Nazir inside the same network.

Khawaja said he did not know anything about the job involving Tom and stated Nazir was not in his employ.

Lee, not his real name, spent a year working for Khawaja as a plumber until, he says, his conscience got the better of him.

"It got a bit too much for me," he said. "I didn't like scamming people. So, I left.

"I've worked for London's biggest plumbing company and, no word of a lie, this lot have more jobs. They're giants."

Rather than relying on solid reputations and recommendation, rogue traders rely on search engine traffic.

They either pay to get their details at the top of Google, which means they are seen first, or they mimic the names of reputable companies by making tiny changes to the business name.

Reached by the BBC's undercover journalist posing as a plumber seeking to work with them, one of Khawaja's associates said: "We're a lead company. We'll send you jobs, and then you go to the jobs.

"We sort the jobs through online advertisement. Usually we'll try and get emergencies so we can charge more. You make up the pricing."

The associate told the undercover reporter they had to charge in the region of £400 for every job, regardless of what work was actually needed.

Both Clive and Tom reported what happened to the Metropolitan Police and Essex Police.

Khawaja said he was not a party to the phone call with the undercover journalist and could not comment on its contents.

He said the alleged statements did not reflect how he operates.

He separately told the BBC in the recorded phone call: "You guys should know I am an entertainer and you guys are taking it out of context."

"I am clearly joking and I'm entertaining and I am engaging with the comments, it is not literal," he added.

He said the right of reply sent to him by the BBC contained "false information which has nothing to do with me".

TikTok said its community guidelines were "clear" and did not "allow any attempts to scam, trick or defraud people".

The firm said in the three months up to June 2026, it had removed 99.2% of content found to be in breach of its "policies on fraud and scams... before it was reported to us".

The BBC put questions to Google including why rogue traders were able to advertise on its platform. It did not answer specific questions, but a Google spokesperson said: "We have strict ads policies that govern the types of ads and advertisers we allow on our platforms.

"Keeping our users and partners safe is our top priority and we invest heavily in the enforcement of our policies.

"We have a team of thousands working around the clock to create and enforce our policies at scale."

Nessar Khawaja, who used the online name ThatGuyNess, regularly posted TikTok videos showing his work as a plumber, explaining how he made thousands of pounds from "desperate" customers,...

articles.title: Jensen Huang: How the Nvidia scandal exposed the risks of Asia's big AI bet
articles.text:
Jensen Huang's extraordinary return as Nvidia's boss rocked not only its shares in New York but also sent shockwaves through the artificial intelligence (AI) industry around the world.

Those jolts were felt particularly in Asia as the saga highlighted the region's huge exposure to the technology.

Tech-heavy stock indexes in Japan, South Korea and Taiwan went on a rollercoaster ride this week. Markets soared after a near-trillion dollar surge in Nvidia's share price but then slumped as concerns about political and regulatory scrutiny hit investor confidence.

The chipmaker is a "symbolic bellwether" of the AI trade that is fast becoming key to places like South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore and Malaysia," says Dylan Loh, an international studies lecturer at Nanyang Technological University.

From chip manufacturing to data centres to foreign investments, AI has become a strategic priority for these economies - and they are now increasingly dependent on Nvidia's fortunes.

In Nvidia, the AI industry has the unrivalled power of cutting-edge chips and the financial clout that turned it into "the bank of AI". And in Huang, it has a high-profile evangelist.

That combination has put it at the heart of the AI ecosystem in more ways than one.

For one, Nvidia was able to grow rapidly by outsourcing chip production instead of having to spend heavily to build its own manufacturing plants.

It contracts out most of its production to Taiwanese chipmaking giant TSMC.

That means Taiwan is vulnerable to changes in AI tech demand, says Paul Cavey, founder of Taipei-based research firm East Asia Econ.

"The surge in [Taiwan's] real economic growth since 2024 has been because of the big increase in AI related exports".

Huang said earlier this year that Nvidia plans to invest around $150bn (£114.4bn) a year in Taiwan at a launch to celebrate the firm's planned headquarters on the island.

To a lesser extent, South Korea and Japan are also exposed to the industry, Cavey adds. They are among its suppliers of key components such as memory chips and testing equipment, with firms like Samsung and SK Hynix making the firm's processors.

On top of that, Nvidia is a financial backstop and major lender to companies in the AI supply chain.

It is difficult to overstate the role Nvidia, with Huang at its helm, has played in the region's AI industry. Nvidia's chips fill its data centres, power its AI models and feed the companies making cars and electronics.

"Asia isn't just a customer base for Nvidia. It is an indispensable engine of the company's AI dominance because of East Asia's semiconductor manufacturing and memory ecosystems," Loh says.

In the Asia-Pacific region, the data centre market, which is largely powered by Nvidia chips, is in the midst of an "unprecedented boom", according to property services firm CBRE, external. The volume of investment has been rising steadily in recent years to reach a record of $11.6bn (£8.85bn) in 2025.

In South East Asia, Singapore-based AI company Megaspeed had become the region's biggest buyer of Nvidia chips before it was accused of smuggling them to China. Megaspeed has said it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation".

The US has said it intends to ban Megaspeed Ltd from doing business in the United States.

But in a timely example of the importance of AI to this region, Singapore this week further raised its growth forecast for this year as the technology boosts its economy.

The world's biggest tech firms - Google, Microsoft, Oracle - also plan to boost their spending on infrastructure in the region by roughly 60% this year, CBRE added.

The demand for neoclouds, which are specialised data centres which power AI, has also risen rapidly, it said.

For economies betting heavily on AI, Nvidia has become "hugely important", with vast sums being spent on its chips and factory activity increasingly dependent on its technology, Loh told the BBC.

In many economies, news of Huang's return to Nvidia was met with jubilation.

In Taiwan, where he was born and the home of "Jensanity", investors jokingly described his return as a "one man saves the village" story.

Social media and groups on messaging platform Line saw posts like "Old Huang is back," while some investors said "Daddy is back to save my life" and "the humanitarian corridor is open."

However, some said the episode should also prompt a closer look at how effective Taiwan has been in building a "non-China" semiconductor supply chain, and how risks from the industry's heavy reliance on Nvidia should be managed better.

Asia's technology industry has been under increasing pressure from the US in recent years. The administrations of both Joe Biden and Donald Trump have tightened rules on the export of Nvidia's most advanced chips to China.

Those efforts seem to have been renewed. Just last week, Washington announced new rules that will increase scrutiny of data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.

The latest move not only restricts the export of high-end chips to China, but also access to their computing power, which Chinese firms currently rent abroad to train AI models.

This will hit South East Asian countries, which have invested billions in data centre infrastructure to cater to Chinese firms. Nvidia has already paused shipments to the region, according to the Financial Times, although it is unclear if this is only a temporary move while it figures out how to comply with the new export rules.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a BBC request for comment.

Then there is the growing bipartisan backlash against President Trump and Nvidia after he said he "made the deal" to "convince" the company‘s board to reinstate Huang.

Huang is also due to testify before Congress next week. And as Democrats prepare to take control of the US House and Senate in the New Year, Huang is likely to face further risks.

"Jensen's return may resolve the immediate leadership crisis, but it does not resolve the legal and political overhangs," said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist from Saxo Bank.

Investor concerns about the trillions of dollars being poured into AI and the pivotal role Nvidia plays in the industry were already sending tremors through global stock markets.

Some fear that while the company and its charismatic leader have been crucial in driving AI's growth that concentration of influence also poses a threat.

Especially now when it appears that Huang's future - which is still uncertain - could impact economies that are heavily exposed to the AI industry.

"I would say the President and White House would love to brush this over and say its fine but I believe Democrats in Congress will definitely be probing", Ray Wang, founder of San Francisco-based Constellation Research said.

"The story is not over yet... Jensen coming back is probably the biggest, baddest return ever. The question is what will happen next?"

Additional reporting by Benny Lu, BBC Chinese

articles.title: Why there's a shortage of lift and escalator mechanics
articles.text:
Some of them are angry. Nerves are frayed. Many of them are just relieved that he's here.

When a lift stops working in Chicago, frazzled building managers might get a visit from Jim Lembesis. For more than 47 years, Lembesis has repaired and upgraded lifts. He says he understands why staff and residents are so anxious to have things working again.

"They wait and they wait," says Lembesis, a field technician for Parkway Elevators. "There's a lot of frustration. Sometimes it's a repeat issue. It's a never-ending cycle, you know what I mean?"

The widely reported shortage of lift and escalator mechanics in the US, which is also a problem in many other countries, has got worse over time, he adds: "It's been like night and day compared to when I started."

Everyone needs a lift now and again. Some people depend on them – elderly residents of high-rise buildings, say, or wheelchair users.

Storm-damaged lifts in Hawaiian apartment blocks this year left some residents trapped, external in their homes for weeks. A lack of mechanics, and problems sourcing parts, were blamed for the repair delays.

In the US, the average salary for a lift mechanic, external is $110,000 (£83,000). And yet people in the industry say it is difficult to attract new workers.

Sure, says Lembesis, you do encounter some dangers in a job like this. There are risks of falling from a great height – or being electrocuted. Once, he was even hit on the head with an umbrella by an elderly lady after he rescued her from a stuck lift.

But there are so many skills to learn, and great camaraderie and knowledge-sharing among mechanics, he says. As one recruiter puts it, these technicians amaze people with their ability to fix things. They are like "wizards". The overall-clad shamans who know how to get modern life running again.

Nine times out of 10, the problem is with the doors, says Lembesis. These components repeatedly move back and forth. "People hit them with carts, and dirt and debris [falls into them]," says Lembesis. "[The doors] take the most beating."

Mechanics often keep various spare door parts in their vehicles, ready to use.

But technicians like Lembesis don't just have to get lifts working, they also have to verify the lifts are safe. He remembers one case, decades ago, getting called out to a burning building. His role was to ensure the lifts, which were being drenched with huge volumes of water, were still safe to use while firefighters tackled the blaze.

"I was there for 15 hours that night," he says. "Everyone, on the way out of the door, shook my hand."

Finding good lift technicians is "becoming more difficult" says Matt Hollinshead, president of the US National Association for Elevator Contractors. "We have a four-year apprenticeship," he says. That's the first hurdle. And many states require certification or licensing before you can work on lifts.

"We have a vast array of equipment that has to be maintained in the United States." Some lifts are 100-years-old. As time goes on, the technological knowledge required to repair them only grows.

Hollinshead says that weeks or months-long delays to lift repairs are not typically due to staff shortages but that, in such cases, it's likely that a particular part isn't readily available. Manufacturing a replacement hydraulic cylinder takes six to 12 weeks, he notes.

But the lack of technicians does mean that that building managers might have to wait days before someone can even diagnose what's wrong with a lift after it stops working.

Hollinshead says teaching the basics of the trade in high schools or technical schools could entice more people into the role.

Matt Allred, a recruiter and host of The Elevator Careers Podcast, emphasises the many skills that lift mechanics require. "You're a little bit of a wizard, right? You show up and if you can fix it – 'Wow!'."

He blames major lift companies, in part, for locking down maintenance contracts, making it difficult or impossible for third-party repairers to intervene when a lift fails.

Two large lift manufacturers approached by BBC News declined interviews. The chief executive of Otis, one of the firms, said in May that her company was struggling to hire enough staff, external to meet demand. The firm also states on its website, external that the shortage of lift mechanics affects "almost every part of the world".

However, a spokesman for Otis claimed its "US talent pipeline" was healthy, and declined an interview.

Everyone else who spoke to BBC News said hiring was challenging in the US. Allred was recently contacted by a major lift company and asked to help them find a technician. "I was surprised that a major company would reach out to a little recruiting shop," he says, suggesting that this reflects the extent of the labour shortage.

That shortage is also a problem in the UK. "It is bad and getting worse," says Dave Cooper, president of the Chartered Institution of Building Services Engineers, who is also chief executive of a lift and escalator engineering consultancy.

"We've known food delivery companies to refuse to deliver to flats above the ground floor because the lift is out of service."

Offering better tax breaks to companies that train lift mechanics could help ensure that plenty of workers continue to enter the industry, he adds.

Training to be a lift mechanic is "not a quick route to competency – and it requires people to stick at it for the long term" says Karen Slade, head of assessment at the Lift and Escalator Industry Association (Leia).

Continued investment in training and attracting new workers is "essential", according to Leia. There are currently 259 active lift and escalator apprentices in the UK, the body adds.

Back in Chicago, Lembesis is working with two younger mechanics who have been "really good", he says, so there's at least some hope for the future.

He stresses again how rewarding he finds his work. The people for whom he fixes lifts tend to be very appreciative.

"I love that. You get that reaction from the customers," he says. "Without them, you got nothing."

articles.title: US approves SpaceX plan to send a million data satellites to space
articles.text:
US regulators have given SpaceX the go-ahead to launch a million satellites into Earth's orbit to help build data centres in space - the first approval of its kind.

The company, which is owned by Elon Musk, wants to use sunlight to power satellites that will process data for AI and send the results back to Earth.

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said on Wednesday that the project, known as Starmind, would "support America's booming super intelligence economy".

However, rival firm Amazon has criticised it as a "lofty ambition rather than a real plan", while astronomers in the US said the move would "significantly undermine" the public's ability to study and observe the night sky.

There is increasing opposition to data centres on earth, including in the US where experts say they were a factor in the Republicans big losses in the midterm elections.

SpaceX believes the "orbital data centres" are the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computing power that is beyond "terrestrial capabilities".

FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement that the project "opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth".

"This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home," Carr said.

Responding to the announcement, Musk wrote on X: "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."

Under the FCC licence, deployment of the satellites must begin no later than November 2033. SpaceX will be required to have deployed 10% by November 2035, rising to 50% by November 2038.

The company has already said it wants to launch its first Starmind satellite next year.

It is unclear whether a million satellites will indeed be launched or whether SpaceX has sought approval for a higher number than it will use.

Like SpaceX's current Starlink network, which provides high-speed internet via more than 10,000 satellites, Starmind's satellites will operate in low-Earth orbit at altitudes ranging between 500-2,000km (310-1,242 miles).

Starmind's satellites will communicate with Starlink's and then relay the data to Earth.

Speaking to the Today programme, on BBC Radio 4, Prof Sir Martin Sweeting, founder and executive chairman of Surrey Satellite Technology Ltd, said while the idea of data centres in space seemed "technically feasible", whether it "makes sense at scale yet" still needed to be analysed.

Being able to get the data from the network of satellites, he added, would depend on being able to use laser links from the ground to them.

"That has not yet been perfected to the level at which it would be able to support the huge amounts of data that are likely to be transferred backwards and forwards," he said.

Meanwhile, the American Astronomical Society (AAS) said it was "disheartened and dismayed" by the decision.

It said the proposed constellation would "significantly undermine decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities" as well as "the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky".

It noted that the constellation "involves larger (and therefore brighter) and more numerous objects", meaning the satellites would "be visible as extremely bright objects for longer periods in the night sky".

Jan Hasselman, a senior attorney at the non-profit group Earthjustice, said in a statement: "Drastically expanding satellites in space has a direct impact on people's everyday lives as well as the future of our planet."

The orbiting data centre concept is also being explored by other firms - including Google and Blue Origin - and is being pitched as a greener alternative to traditional centres, which require enormous amounts of power to run and water for cooling.

The ever-expanding use of AI computing has seen a massive increase in the amount of data that needs to be stored and processed around the world.

New facilities continue to be built but it is becoming difficult to find places to put them. Data centres are large and sprawling, use enormous amounts of power and water for cooling, and increasingly local people don't want them built nearby.

An expert previously told the BBC that launching hardware into orbit remains expensive and that the infrastructure to protect, cool and power them can be complex - while a growing quantity of space debris puts the physical hardware at risk.

Separately, another cautioned that the growing number of low-orbit craft increases the possibility of crashes between objects - which could damage machines or send materials falling back to earth.

Starlink has been accused of creating congestion in space, something Musk denies. He has also rejected claims his satellites have been taking up too much room and crowding out competitors.

articles.title: Huawei found guilty of stealing US trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering
articles.text:
Huawei has been found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but not guilty of the more serious overarching racketeering charge in a landmark case in the US.

In a two-month trial, prosecutors accused the Chinese technology and telecommunications giant of lying, cheating and stealing to gain any competitive advantage.

Huawei's defence team argued that prosecutors had decided Huawei was a criminal organisation and built its case from there, but the firm's success was due to its own innovation.

Huawei said, external the racketeering acquittal "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis", adding that it would "take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests".

Jurors in a Brooklyn court found Huawei guilty of 10 out of 12 counts, which included conspiracy to violate US sanctions.

However, the jury declined to convict Huawei of the racketeering conspiracy charge, which required members to find the firm acted like a criminal enterprise.

Federal prosecutors first announced the charges against Huawei in 2019, after the dramatic arrest in late 2018 of senior executive Meng Wanzhou in Canada.

Meng, also known as Cathy Meng, was held for three years in Canada before she was released to return to China through a deal with US prosecutors.

During closing arguments last week, assistant US attorney Meredith Arfa told jurors Huawei spent 20 years doing whatever it took to expand its business, including lying to banks about its business dealings in Iran and stealing technology secrets from rival firms to ensure it had a competitive edge.

"For decades, Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted their business in the United States on the basis of lies and theft," US Attorney General Todd Blanche said in statement, external.

"Thanks to the work of the FBI and our federal prosecutors, those who engaged in these criminal activities will be held accountable."

The Chinese government hit out at what it called the US "suppression" of Chinese companies and said it supports Chinese firms protecting their interests.

Defence attorney Brian Heberlig said it was by dint of hard work that Huawei's business had expanded with operations in 170 countries and more than 200,000 staff.

Following the verdict, Heberlig told the BBC that Huawei was gratified that the jury had rejected the racketeering charge.

"The RICO [Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act] count that alleged that Huawei was a corrupt organisation, with a corporate culture and policy of committing crime. That was, in our view, a significant overreach, and the jury soundly rejected it," he said.

"Of course, we have mixed emotions about the rest of the verdict ... [we] thought that Huawei was deserving of acquittals across the board."

Sentencing is planned for September 2027. Heberlig said there will be "significant advocacy" to achieve the lowest sentence possible. Following that, he said he fully expects Huawei to appeal.

"If I know Huawei, that fight will continue, and the company's not going to rest until it's pursued every last argument it can through appeal, and hopefully, ultimately toward vindication," he said.

articles.title: EA adds AI-generated John Motson to FC 27 video game
articles.text:
Football game EA Sports FC will feature the digitally recreated voice of the late commentator John Motson, Electronic Arts has exclusively told the BBC.

Motson, who died in 2023, was the main commentator for BBC Sport for decades - and performed the same role for the video game series during the 90s and 00s.

It is the first time the hit series, formerly known as Fifa, has featured a deceased commentator.

With the permission of his widow and his son, Motson's voice has been synthesised using a combination of old recording sessions and generative AI. It will become available in FC 27 on 26 November.

The legendary commentator died aged 77 in February 2023 - several months after the launch of ChatGPT and the massive growth of AI it set in train.

Fred Motson told the BBC it "means an awful lot" to have his dad's voice in EA Sports FC once again.

"I grew up with Fifa," he said. "I always used to tell my parents that I needed the latest console for Christmas because otherwise dad couldn't see how the game worked."

Electronic Arts, which was bought for $55bn (£42bn) in August, told the BBC it paid Motson's family for the rights to use his likeness and recreate his voice, but would not disclose the financial terms of the deal.

The BBC's lead football commentator Guy Mowbray said it was a "privilege" to be involved in the game, which he has provided commentary for since 2023.

"I think it's quite a nice, sort of non-scary use of AI," he said.

"We're in the business of nostalgia... I hear commentary not in my own voice, but in John's voice, because that's the voice I knew growing up.

"So I think it's nice that that legacy can be continued in this way."

John Motson was the first commentator for the series, appearing on games from Fifa 96 up to Fifa 2005. He later made a brief cameo in Fifa 19.

"While he completely understood when they went in a different direction, I think he really missed it after he left the game and it felt like a bit of an end of an era," his son said.

EA told the BBC the studio would not have included Motson in the game unless they had permission from his family.

"There was no way we would have moved forward with this in any way, shape or form if they weren't fully on board," said Mat Prior, senior game design director at EA Sports FC.

"At the outset we wanted to pay tribute to Motty as the commentator and as this emotional connection - he was the very first voice of our game - so we really wanted to do him justice and bring him back."

He explained that Motson's voice in the game was a combination of old lines he recorded over the years and AI - tech which he said was "the only way" to make it happen, as they don't have recordings of him talking about modern players like Bradley Barcola and Chloe Kelly.

Motson's son Fred said he believed his dad would have "absolutely" wanted to be involved in the game after his death.

"My dad was the least technological person in the world," he said. "Till his dying day, he had a typewriter on his desk.

"So I don't think he would have quite understood what the AI was doing technologically - but I think, on the other hand, he was always really keen to get involved in these kinds of projects."

But Peter Caulfield, founder of Save Our Voices Now which campaigns against AI voice cloning, expressed some disquiet about the project, and the fact Motson had been unable to consent to it.

"If someone has signed a deal allowing their likeness to be used after they die, I have no issue with that," he said.

"But in life or in death, unless you have specifically agreed to it, AI cloning of any kind should not be allowed.

"Being a family member shouldn't automatically give you that right either."

One of the main arguments against the use of generative AI in video games is that it can replace humans - something that EA was keen to argue against.

"From a gaming standpoint, it's something we've used for many years - like machine learning to help drive animation systems and so on and so forth," Prior said.

"It's not there to replace commentators in any way shape or form... there's certainly no future plans to replace anyone with AI."

Derek Rae, who has been a commentator in EA FC for several years, said the tech could make things easier, but he still spent a long time recording dialogue in studios.

"It's quite a lot of days in the course of a year," he said. "So it might be two or three times a month that we do it in season for the game, which is typically sort of November time through until May.

"The more creative things have to be done with the human voice because they have to have the personality, sometimes a little chuckle thrown in the middle of a sentence or a little idiosyncrasy," he said.

"But when it comes to the more normal features in a video game, for example, routine surnames like Smith and Jones and Brown, that's something that AI can probably accomplish quite easily."

articles.title: Zoe Kleinman: Nobody is irreplaceable - unless you're Jensen Huang
articles.text:
Remember the tech boss and his head of HR, both married to other people, who were caught on camera at a Coldplay concert with their arms wrapped around each other?

Their horrified reaction went viral, and the pair both resigned. Astronomer, the firm where they both worked, said their actions had fallen short of its standards.

Compared with the scandal which has engulfed Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang in recent weeks, that Coldplay kiss cam moment now feels rather tame.

Huang admitted to having had an affair, reportedly with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy.

There were suggestions that she may have been involved in smuggling Nvidia chips into China, in breach of a US export ban.

Concerns about national security had reached the desk of US President Donald Trump.

There were other stories about some of Huang's relationships with female colleagues.

For most of us, that would without question amount to instant, and irreversible, dismissal.

But while Huang briefly left the company, he was just as swiftly reinstated, and welcomed back with open arms.

As I watched footage of him being greeted with cheers, applause, high fives and a big hug back at the company's HQ on Monday, I wondered how many disgraced bosses would kill to be in his shoes.

"Imagine being that Coldplay CEO reading all the comments on here about how it's OK if you're actually a good enough CEO," quipped menswear writer Derek Guy on X, external.

Huang has blown out of the water the old adage that nobody is irreplaceable.

Despite names of potential permanent replacements being bandied around, Nvidia's board evidently reached the same conclusion - interim chief executive Colette Kress was in for less than two weeks.

So how on Earth did he manage it?

Well firstly, Huang is the boss of a company that has manoeuvred itself into a uniquely powerful position.

Nvidia's computer chips are considered the best in the business for driving AI.

Demand for its latest tech is through the roof and the firm sets its prices accordingly: Its Rubin and Vera GPUs sell for tens of thousands of dollars each, and one data centre might contain hundreds of them.

So, the US AI sector relies on Nvidia, Trump is determined that the American AI industry needs to be the best in the world, and Huang is the only leader the company has ever known.

He's been at the helm for 33 years and he's a computer scientist himself, renowned for being very hands-on with the development process. (Whether the boss's input is always wanted is another matter, but it's always there.)

Working for Huang isn't easy.

Long hours are normal and negative feedback is often given in front of everyone else.

When he wants something to happen, he doesn't stop until it does: one of his early ideas was to halve the chip production cycle, in order to get one step ahead of the competition with their longer lead times for orders.

Lots of experts told him it couldn't be done. Until eventually, they did it.

Not only does Huang have technical expertise, he's also a charismatic figurehead, representing Nvidia at events around the world in his trademark leather jacket, rubbing shoulders with world leaders, royalty, and fellow tech bosses.

For many, he's become something of a cult figure. Nvidia sometimes sells limited edition clothing at conference pop up stalls. A jumper featuring a cartoon image of Huang costs $178 (£137).

Huang's brief departure from Nvidia caused economic turmoil. The firm's value sank by a whopping $1tn before it climbed back up again.

It affected not only pension funds and investors around the world, but also Nvidia's own staff.

Tech employees often get to own valuable stocks in the company they work for as part of their pay packages.

Nvidia employees have been sitting on a goldmine. It wasn't really in their interests to see that drain away because of the boss's love life.

With a firm grip on the company he co-founded, cult-like status in tech circles and friends in high places, Jensen Huang created a situation where even national security concerns over the US's biggest rival couldn't topple him.

articles.title: US attorney general dodges questions about Nvidia investigation
articles.text:
US Attorney General Todd Blanche has backed Nvidia as a "good corporate citizen" while refusing to comment on whether the AI chipmaker was under federal investigation.

Blanche said he had no information about newly reinstated CEO Jensen Huang's security clearance status, as lawmakers demand answers about US President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's comeback.

Huang was given his job back less than two weeks after being forced to resign over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

Asked several times on Tuesday whether the justice department or FBI had investigated Huang, Blanche responded: "I don't know what you're talking about."

Huang is still set to appear before Congress next week, where he will be questioned about national security concerns over his relationship with an alleged spy who previously ran Megaspeed, a Singapore-based corporate customer of Nvidia.

Trump has said he would consider pardoning Huang for any potential criminal activity, though he does not think it will come to that.

"It's always an option, I guess, but I don't think it'll be necessary," Trump told the New York Post in an interview published on Tuesday.

The US commerce department has also announced it was preparing to blacklist the tech company Megaspeed, which has been suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China.

The commerce and justice departments said last week that they began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations".

But Blanche told reporters on Tuesday that the latter had "hundreds, if not more" export investigations occurring at any one time.

"So when you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don't know what you're talking about," he said.

Asked if he was satisfied Nvidia had been co-operative with inquiries into whether it or Huang knew about chips being diverted to China, Blanche said: "I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen.

"Obviously, if Nvidia was the target or was subject to some criminal investigation or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn't be the message that the president is saying to the American people.

"It shouldn't be what my message would be either."

While Nvidia's stock market value surged on the announcement of Huang's reappointment, some of the gains were reversed in volatile Tuesday trading.

The company's share price closed down nearly 6% - still well above where it ended last week. On Monday, Nvidia stock rocketed more than 31% following news of Huang's return.

Huang reportedly apologised to Nvidia employees on Tuesday, the day after returning to the company as chief executive, saying he had made "terrible mistakes" and was now receiving daily 90-minute therapy sessions.

articles.title: Why tiny cars are taking off across Europe
articles.text:
Selena Buse, 16, reverses her Citroën Ami out of a parking space and heads off past the school playground. Heads turn. The Ami looks pretty remarkable. Futurist or like-a-toaster depending on your point of view. But it's changed her life.

"I got it because I really needed it to get to school. And I use it to visit friends on the weekends. It's indispensable in rural areas like where I live," she says.

In France, you can drive a car like this from the age of 14 with a road safety certificate and eight hours training. In Italy too.

In Germany and Spain it's 15, in the UK 16, external. Because they are classed as motorised quadri-cycles. Four-wheel mopeds in other words.

Registrations have risen from about 13,000 in 2019 to around 25,000 last year in France.

In Europe, sales have gone from 30,000 to 60,000 in the past five years. And the Ami, launched in 2020, has really changed the image, with teenagers who now account for a quarter of all mini-car sales.

In Selena's very small Citroën, we are soon rolling along at the top speed of 45km/h (28mph). For other road users, no-licence cars like this can seem like mobile traffic calming.

"When I'm on faster roads and there's a lot of traffic the cars behind me sometimes honk their horns but I can't go any quicker!" Selena says.

Another local Daniel Laprès, who drives a micro-car made by French firm and market-leader Aixam, tells me he actually pulls over to let the cars behind pass.

He and his wife moved from Paris to this country village two years ago. Of Canadian nationality, he didn't swap his foreign licence for a French one in time and lost the right to drive. That didn't matter much when he was in Paris. Like many Parisians he didn't need a car. He used public transport. But that's not possible here.

"We tried living off of taxis and it was in the end a disaster. Then we heard about how you could drive without having to have a licence, and it was the exact solution to our problem. Cheap, inexpensive to operate, basically no administrative formalities, you get insurance."

However, Laprès feels less safe in his small car. "They're little more than tin cans on wheels, right? I mean, you're not going to be driving fast, but someone else could be."

These cars are forbidden on motorways and on faster highways.

By mistake Laprès found himself on a main road with a 110km/h speed limit, which slow vehicles are not allowed on.

"I did it once and I will never, ever do it again. On those roads everybody is passing you, including the biggest trucks. And they come at you very fast from the rear, so it's scary," Laprès says.

Daniel is 77 so fits in with the long-established market for these cars: older people living in the countryside.

Traditionally the market also included quite a few people who'd lost their licences, often because of drink-driving offences. But the launch of the electric Citroën Ami in 2020 changed the customer profile and the product.

"The launch of the Ami was the beginning of the transformation of the sector, with more and more electric models coming on to the market. In 2026, more than 67% of new licence-free cars are electric," says Marie-Laure Nivot, market analyst at AAA Data.

Meanwhile, the competition is producing increasingly sophisticated minicars - some costing as much as a small conventional car. At Ligier, marketing director Romain Illegems says the biggest change is in who's buying them.

"We've gone from mobility that was imposed on people to mobility that people choose. Before, these vehicles were something you used because you absolutely needed to get around, because there was no public transport, or because you didn't have a licence.

"Today, teenagers are choosing them instead of scooters or mopeds, because they're safer and offer better protection from the weather. Young people now account for 40% of our customers."

There are limitations, of course. Just two seats, a maximum speed of 45km/h and no motorways. But for Selena, who rents her Ami for €60 a month, plus insurance, it's a small price to pay for independence.

Clarification 27 November: This article was amended to clarify that Mr Laprès accidentally drove on a highway that his car was not permitted on.
